docs.title: Data Platform Lab
docs.text:
A hands-on engineering lab for understanding how modern data platforms actually work — from Spark execution to Iceberg internals and analytical databases.

Modern data platforms are built from many layers: distributed execution engines, storage formats, metadata systems, analytical databases, and orchestration tools.

This repository documents my journey of understanding these systems from first principles—not by memorizing frameworks, but by uncovering the engineering trade-offs behind them.

docs.title: Who is this for?
docs.text:
This notebook is intended for engineers who already have some familiarity with modern data tooling and want to understand:

  • Why Parquet became the dominant analytical storage format.
  • How Spark executes distributed workloads.
  • Why Hive breaks at scale.
  • How Iceberg solves metadata and consistency problems.
  • How analytical databases such as ClickHouse achieve low-latency queries.
  • How all these components fit together to form a modern Data Platform.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This repository deliberately skips introductory material.

There is already excellent documentation explaining:

  • What Spark is.
  • What Docker and containers are.
  • Basic SQL concepts.
  • Kafka fundamentals.
  • Object storage basics.
  • The APIs of individual technologies.

The focus here is different:

How do these systems actually work internally, and why were they designed this way?

To get the most value from these notes, you should already be comfortable with:

  • Software engineering fundamentals.
  • Linux and containers.
  • Basic SQL.
  • Distributed systems concepts.
  • Reading code and technical documentation.

docs.title: Recommended Learning Path
docs.text: The chapters are designed to be followed in order.

docs.text:

docs.text:

Move beyond files and understand table formats:

  • Time travel
  • Schema evolution

docs.text:

docs.title: Philosophy
docs.text:
This repository intentionally focuses on engineering intuition over framework APIs.

The goal is not to learn how to call a library.

The goal is to answer questions such as:

  • Why does Spark shuffle?
  • Why are Parquet row groups important?
  • Why do analytical databases sort data?
  • Why does Hive struggle with large metadata volumes?
  • Why does Iceberg exist?
  • How do OLAP engines achieve interactive query performance?

docs.title: Repository Structure
docs.text:
Fundamentals → Spark → Lakehouse → ClickHouse
                      ↓
              Experiments & Notebooks

The emphasis is on building a mental model that connects the entire stack rather than learning each technology in isolation.

docs.title: 1.1 A System That Should Have Worked
docs.text:
Imagine you’ve just built a data platform.

Nothing fancy — but not small either.

  • Events flowing in at a few million per second
  • ClickHouse cluster sitting behind ingestion
  • Queries running dashboards, aggregations, reports

For the first few weeks, everything feels… effortless.

  • Ingestion is smooth
  • Queries are fast
  • CPU utilization is modest
  • Storage is growing, but predictably

You feel confident.

Then, slowly, something starts to change.

Not dramatically. Not suddenly. But enough to make you uneasy.

  • IO starts creeping up
  • Some queries feel slower
  • Background tasks seem more active
  • Disk and network graphs look noisier

You scale the cluster slightly. Things improve. Temporarily.

Then it comes back.

docs.title: 1.2 The First Wrong Explanation
docs.text:
At this point, most engineers reach for a familiar explanation:

“We’re ingesting more data, so IO is higher.”

That sounds reasonable.

But pause for a moment.

You check the numbers.

  • Ingestion rate: stable
  • Query load: roughly the same
  • CPU: not saturated

So if:

  • You’re not ingesting significantly more
  • You’re not querying significantly more

Then why is IO increasing?

docs.title: 1.3 A Subtle Observation
docs.text:
You dig deeper.

You notice something interesting.

The system is doing a lot of background work — even when query load is low.

There are processes that:

  • Read data
  • Write data
  • Delete data

But you’re not issuing those operations explicitly.

They’re happening… on their own.

docs.title: 🤔 Pause Here
docs.text:
Before reading further, try to answer:

If you insert data once, why would the system need to read and rewrite it again?

Take a moment. This is the key question.

docs.title: 1.4 The Hidden Mechanism
docs.text:
What you’re seeing is not incidental behavior.

It is the core design of ClickHouse.

When you insert data into a MergeTree table:

  • The data is written as a part
  • That part is immutable
  • It is sorted according to ORDER BY
  • It is immediately queryable

So far, nothing unusual.

But over time, many such parts accumulate.

And here’s the critical detail:

ClickHouse does not keep those parts as-is forever.

Instead, it periodically performs merges.

docs.title: 1.5 What a Merge Really Is
docs.text:
A merge is not a metadata operation.

It is not a pointer update.

It is a full data rewrite.

When ClickHouse merges parts:

  1. It reads multiple existing parts
  2. It decompresses their data
  3. It merges them into a single sorted stream
  4. It writes a new part
  5. It deletes the old parts

Let that sink in.

Every merge is:

  • A read of existing data
  • A write of new data

docs.title: 1.6 The First Realization
docs.text:
Go back to your earlier assumption:

“We write data once.”

That is no longer true.

In reality:

  • Data is written once during ingestion
  • Then rewritten multiple times during merges

So the system is not just storing data.

It is continuously reorganizing it.

docs.title: 🤔 Pause Again
docs.text:
If a row is:

  • Written once during insert
  • Then rewritten 3 more times during merges

How many times did that row hit disk?

docs.title: 1.7 The Amplification Effect
docs.text:
If you follow that through:

  • 1 initial write
  • 3 rewrite as part of merge

That’s 4 total writes.

Which means:

Your system may be writing 3–5× more data than you ingest.

And that extra IO?

It doesn’t show up in your ingestion metrics.

But it absolutely shows up in:

  • Disk bandwidth
  • Object storage requests
  • Network utilization

docs.title: 1.8 Why This Design Exists
docs.text:
At this point, a natural reaction is:

“Why would a database do this? This seems wasteful.”

But the design is deliberate.

By rewriting data, ClickHouse achieves:

docs.title: 1. Better Compression
docs.text:
When small parts are merged:

  • Similar values cluster together
  • Encoding becomes more effective
  • Storage footprint reduces

docs.title: 2. Better Query Performance
docs.text:
Larger, well-merged parts mean:

  • Fewer files to scan
  • Better locality
  • More effective skipping

docs.title: 3. Simpler Write Path
docs.text:
Because:

  • Inserts are append-only
  • No in-place updates
  • No locking complexity

So the system trades:

  • Write amplification for
  • Read efficiency and simplicity

docs.title: 1.9 The Mental Model Shift
docs.text:
This leads to a fundamental shift in how you think about the system.

ClickHouse is not:

“A system that stores data efficiently”

It is:

“A system that continuously rewrites data to maintain efficient structure”

docs.title: 1.10 The Consequence You Must Internalize
docs.text:
Once you accept this, many things become clearer:

  • Why IO grows even if ingestion is stable
  • Why small design mistakes explode at scale
  • Why merges dominate system behavior
  • Why “just adding more data” changes system dynamics

docs.title: 1.11 The Core Equation
docs.text:
You can now express system IO as:

Total IO = Ingestion IO + Merge Rewrite IO

And crucially:

Merge Rewrite IO is often the dominant term.

docs.title: 1.12 Stress the Model
docs.text:
Let’s test your understanding.

Imagine:

  • You completely disable merges (hypothetically)

What happens?

Pause and think.

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
At first:

  • IO drops
  • System looks stable

But over time:

  • Parts accumulate
  • Queries slow down
  • Metadata explodes
  • Skipping becomes ineffective

Eventually:

The system collapses from fragmentation instead of IO.

docs.title: 1.13 The Balanced View
docs.text:
So merges are:

  • Necessary for performance
  • Expensive in IO

And the entire system becomes a balancing act:

Enough merges to keep data efficient

But not so many that IO overwhelms the system

docs.title: 1.14 Closing Insight
docs.text:
If you take only one thing from this chapter, let it be this:

ClickHouse does not store data once.

It rewrites it repeatedly to maintain structure.

Everything you will learn next — parts, partitions, batching, amplification, IO limits — flows from this single truth.

docs.title: The Hidden Cost Of The Inserts
2.1 Two Teams, Same Data, Different Outcomes
docs.text:
Let’s start with a simple setup.

Two teams are building ingestion pipelines into ClickHouse.

Both teams ingest exactly the same data:

  • Same schema
  • Same volume (say, 1 billion rows per day)
  • Same query patterns

From a business perspective, these systems are identical.

docs.title: Team A
docs.text:
They ingest data as it arrives:

  • Each event → one insert
  • Continuous, real-time writes

docs.title: Team B
docs.text:
They batch data:

  • Buffer events
  • Insert in chunks of ~100,000 rows

After a few weeks, something strange happens.

docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
Team A:

  • Merge backlog increasing
  • IO constantly high
  • Query latency degrading
  • System feels “noisy”

Team B:

  • Stable IO
  • Predictable merges
  • Queries still fast

docs.title: 🤔 Pause Here
docs.text:
Both systems ingest the same number of rows.

So ask yourself:

Why is one system unstable while the other is healthy?

Take a moment. Don’t rush.

docs.title: 2.2 The First Instinct (and Why It Fails)
docs.text:
A common explanation is:

“Maybe Team A has more queries.”

But we already controlled for that.

Another guess:

“Maybe their data distribution is different.”

Also controlled.

So what’s left?

docs.title: 2.3 A Subtle Difference
docs.text:
The only difference is:

  • How the data is inserted

Let’s zoom into that.

docs.title: 2.4 What Happens on Insert (Revisited Carefully)
docs.text:
From Chapter 1, you know:

  • Every insert creates a part
  • That part is immutable
  • Merges later combine parts

Now, let’s connect this to the two teams.

docs.title: Team A
docs.text:
• 1 row per insert
  • → 1 part per insert

If they ingest 1 million rows:

  • They create 1 million parts

docs.title: Team B
docs.text:
• 100k rows per insert
  • → 1 part per insert

For the same 1 million rows:

  • They create 10 parts

docs.title: 🤔 Pause Again
docs.text:
Same data.

But:

  • Team A → 1,000,000 parts
  • Team B → 10 parts

What does that imply for merges?

docs.title: 2.5 The Explosion You Don’t See
docs.text:
Let’s think about merges now.

Merges combine parts.

So if you have:

  • 10 parts → a few merges
  • 1,000,000 parts → enormous merge work

But the deeper problem is not just count.

docs.title: 2.6 The Real Metric (This Is Critical)
docs.text:
At this point, most people still think in:

“rows per second”

ClickHouse doesn’t care about that as much as you think.

The system actually scales with:

parts per second

Let’s define it:

parts/sec = inserts/sec × partitions_touched

In this scenario:

  • Team A → extremely high inserts/sec → very high parts/sec
  • Team B → low inserts/sec → low parts/sec

docs.title: 💡 First Major Insight
docs.text: ClickHouse is constrained by how many parts you create, not how many rows you insert.

docs.title: 2.7 Why Parts Are Expensive (Beyond Count)
docs.text:
Let’s go deeper.

Each part is not just “some rows.”

Each part carries:

  • Its own primary index
  • Its own metadata
  • Its own files in storage
  • Its own lifecycle in merges

So when you increase parts:

You increase:

  • Metadata in memory
  • Number of files / objects
  • Merge scheduling complexity
  • IO operations

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text:
If each part is a unit of work:

What happens when you create too many units of work per second?

docs.title: 2.8 The System Falls Behind
docs.text:
Let’s connect this to the core equation from Chapter 1:

part_creation_rate <= merge_compaction_rate

docs.title: Team A
docs.text:
• part_creation_rate → extremely high
  • merge_compaction_rate → limited by IO

So:

part_creation_rate > merge_compaction_rate

Result:

  • Parts accumulate
  • Merge backlog grows
  • IO increases (more rewrites needed)
  • System destabilizes

docs.title: Team B
docs.text:
• part_creation_rate → low
  • merge_compaction_rate → sufficient

So:

part_creation_rate <= merge_compaction_rate

Result:

  • Parts get merged efficiently
  • System stays stable

docs.title: 2.9 The Hidden Non-Linearity
docs.text:
Here’s the subtle but powerful realization:

Doubling rows does not necessarily double system cost.

But doubling parts can explode system cost.

Because:

  • Parts drive merge work
  • Merge work drives IO
  • IO drives system stability

docs.title: 2.10 Continuous Ingestion — The Real Trap
docs.text:
Now let’s make this more realistic.

You might say:

“We don’t insert one row at a time — we have streaming pipelines.”

Fair.

But even in streaming systems:

  • Micro-batch size matters
  • Insert frequency matters

If your pipeline produces:

  • Very frequent small batches

You are effectively recreating Team A’s problem.

docs.title: 2.11 The Illusion of Real-Time
docs.text:
There’s a trap here.

Engineers often think:

“Lower latency ingestion is always better.”

So they reduce batch size.

But in ClickHouse:

Ultra-low latency ingestion can destroy system stability.

Because:

  • You increase inserts/sec
  • Which increases parts/sec
  • Which increases merge pressure

docs.title: 💡 Second Major Insight
docs.text: There is a tradeoff between ingestion latency and system stability.

docs.title: 2.12 A Deeper Thought Experiment
docs.text: Imagine two systems:

docs.title: System X
docs.text:
• 10M rows/sec
  • Batch size = 1M
  • → 10 inserts/sec

docs.title: System Y
docs.text:
• 1M rows/sec
  • Batch size = 1
  • → 1M inserts/sec

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: Which system is more likely to fail?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
System Y — despite lower data volume.

Because:

  • Parts/sec is enormous
  • Merge system collapses

docs.title: 2.13 The Real Control Lever
docs.text:
At this point, you can identify the most powerful lever:

Batch size

Not:

  • Hardware
  • Schema
  • Index

But:

How much data you group per insert

docs.title: 2.14 Why Increasing Batch Size Works
docs.text:
When you increase batch size:

  • Parts/sec ↓
  • Merge frequency ↓
  • Merge amplification ↓
  • IO ↓

You’re not reducing data.

You’re reducing work units.

docs.title: 2.15 Stress the Model Again
docs.text:
Suppose:

  • You increase batch size 10×
  • Parts/sec drops 10×

What happens?

Pause.

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
• Merge backlog reduces
  • IO reduces
  • System stabilizes

Even though:

  • Total data remains the same

docs.title: 2.16 The Bigger Picture
docs.text:
You now have two foundational truths:

From Chapter 1:

Data is rewritten multiple times

From Chapter 2:

The number of parts controls how much rewriting happens

Combine them:

Parts control amplification → amplification controls IO → IO controls stability

docs.title: 2.17 Closing Insight
docs.text:
If you remember only one thing from this chapter:

ClickHouse does not scale with rows.

It scales with how intelligently you batch those rows into parts.

docs.title: 3.1 A System That Looks “Almost Fine”
docs.text:
Let’s construct a scenario.

You’ve already learned your lesson from Chapter 2.

So you are not inserting one row at a time.

Instead:

  • Batch size: ~50,000 rows
  • Ingestion: steady
  • Partitioning: time-based (reasonable)

On paper, this should be fine.

And initially — it is.

After a few days:

  • System is stable
  • Queries are fast
  • Merges are happening

But as data grows:

  • Merge backlog slowly increases
  • IO usage keeps creeping up
  • Some queries degrade

Nothing catastrophic. Just… uncomfortable.

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text:
You’re already batching.

So ask yourself:

Why is the system still struggling?

docs.title: 3.2 The First Wrong Explanation
docs.text:
A common reaction:

“Maybe we need more hardware.”

That might help temporarily.

But you already know from Chapter 1:

IO problems often come from amplification, not raw volume.

So adding hardware may just delay the problem.

docs.title: 3.3 Looking Deeper: What Is a “Small Part”?
docs.text:
We need to define this carefully.

A “small part” is not about rows alone.

It is about:

  • Total size (MB/GB)
  • Number of granules
  • How much work it represents in merges

For example:

  • 50k rows might be:
    • ~5–20 MB (depending on schema)

That is tiny in analytical systems.

docs.title: 3.4 Why Size Matters More Than You Think
docs.text:
Let’s imagine your system is continuously creating these small parts.

Every second:

  • New 50k-row parts arrive
  • Merge system starts working

Now, think about how parts evolve.

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: If you start with many small parts, how do you get to large parts?

docs.title: 3.5 The Merge Ladder
docs.text:
Parts don’t jump from small → huge instantly.

They grow gradually:

Level 0: 50k rows
Level 1: 200k rows
Level 2: 800k rows
Level 3: 3M rows
Level 4: 12M rows
...

Each level requires a merge.

Each merge requires:

  • Reading input parts
  • Writing output part

docs.title: 3.6 The Hidden Cost: Depth
docs.text:
Now we arrive at the real issue.

Small parts don’t just increase count.

They increase merge depth.

docs.title: 🤔 Think Carefully
docs.text:
If you start with:

  • Very small parts → many levels needed
  • Larger parts → fewer levels needed

Which system rewrites data more times?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text: The one with smaller parts.

docs.title: 3.7 From Count to Amplification
docs.text:
Let’s connect this with Chapter 1.

If each level rewrites data:

  • Small parts → more levels → more rewrites
  • Large parts → fewer levels → fewer rewrites

So:

smaller parts → higher amplification

docs.title: 3.8 A Concrete Example
docs.text: Let’s make this tangible.

docs.title: Case A — Small Parts
docs.text:
Start with 50k rows per part:

  • Need ~5 merge levels to reach large part
  • Each row rewritten ~5 times

docs.title: Case B — Larger Parts
docs.text:
Start with 500k rows per part:

  • Need ~2 merge levels
  • Each row rewritten ~2 times

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text:
Same data.

Which system generates more IO?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text: Case A — significantly more.

docs.title: 3.9 The Compounding Effect
docs.text:
Here’s the subtlety:

This is not linear.

It compounds.

Because:

  • More parts → more merges
  • More merges → more IO
  • More IO → slower merges
  • Slower merges → backlog grows
  • Backlog → even more parts

This is a feedback loop.

docs.title: 3.10 The System Spiral
docs.text:
Let’s describe the failure mode:

  1. Small parts created frequently
  2. Merge system tries to catch up
  3. IO increases
  4. Merge speed drops (IO contention)
  5. Parts accumulate
  6. Even more merges required
  7. System enters unstable state

docs.title: 💡 Key Insight
docs.text:
Small parts don’t just increase work.

They create a self-reinforcing instability loop.

docs.title: 3.11 Why This Is Worse in Object Storage
docs.text:
(We’ll go deeper later, but a preview)

Each part:

  • Is a set of files / objects
  • Requires network IO
  • Has latency overhead

So:

  • More parts → more requests
  • More requests → more latency
  • More latency → slower merges

Small parts amplify this effect.

docs.title: 3.12 The Misleading Stability Phase
docs.text:
This is important.

Small parts don’t break the system immediately.

They:

  • Work fine at small scale
  • Gradually degrade
  • Fail only after accumulation

This is why teams often:

“Don’t see the problem coming”

docs.title: 3.13 The Real Definition of “Healthy”
docs.text:
A healthy system is not:

  • Low CPU
  • Fast queries

A healthy system is:

Parts are growing steadily into larger sizes

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text:
If you observe:

  • Many small parts
  • Few large parts

What does that indicate?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Merge pipeline is not progressing.

System is at risk.

docs.title: 3.14 The Correct Lever (Revisited)
docs.text:
At this point, the solution becomes clearer.

To fix small-part problems:

  • Increase batch size
  • Reduce parts/sec
  • Ensure parts start larger

Not:

  • Change ORDER BY
  • Add indexes
  • Tune queries

docs.title: 3.15 Stress Test
docs.text:
Suppose:

  • You double batch size
  • Parts become 2× larger

What happens?

Pause.

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
• Merge levels reduce
  • Rewrite count reduces
  • IO reduces
  • System stabilizes

docs.title: 3.16 The Deep Connection
docs.text:
Now connect Chapters 1–3:

  • Chapter 1: Data is rewritten
  • Chapter 2: Parts control merge workload
  • Chapter 3: Part size controls rewrite depth

docs.title: 3.17 Final Mental Model
docs.text:
You can now think of the system as:

Insert → Parts → Merge Levels → IO → Stability

And the most powerful lever is:

Part size at creation

docs.title: 3.18 Closing Insight
docs.text:
If you remember one thing:

Small parts are dangerous not because they are many,

but because they force the system to rewrite data many more times.

docs.title: 4.1 A System That Defies Intuition
docs.text:
Let’s begin with a situation that feels… wrong.

You observe a ClickHouse cluster:

  • Ingestion rate: 600 MB/sec
  • Query load: moderate
  • CPU usage: not maxed

But your monitoring shows:

  • Disk IO: 2.5–3 GB/sec sustained

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text:
Where is the extra IO coming from?

You’re only ingesting 600 MB/sec.

No massive queries.

So why is the system pushing ~3 GB/sec?

docs.title: 4.2 The First Wrong Answer
docs.text:
Most people say:

“Maybe queries are scanning a lot.”

You check.

They aren’t.

Another guess:

“Replication traffic?”

Assume for now — single replica.

Still doesn’t explain it.

So we’re left with something uncomfortable:

The system is doing work you didn’t explicitly ask for.

docs.title: 4.3 Recalling What We Learned
docs.text:
From Chapter 1:

  • Data is rewritten during merges

From Chapter 3:

  • Smaller parts → more rewrite passes

Now we quantify that.

docs.title: 4.4 The Concept of Amplification
docs.text:
Let’s define a term:

Merge Amplification Factor

This represents:

How many times data is rewritten after initial ingestion.

docs.title: 4.5 A Thought Experiment
docs.text:
Imagine a single row:

  • Written once during insert
  • Rewritten 3 times during merges

Total writes:

1 (insert) + 3 (merges) = 4 writes

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text:
If your system ingests 600 MB/sec…

And each byte is rewritten 4 times…

What is total IO?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
600 MB/sec × 4 = 2.4 GB/sec

That matches your observation.

docs.title: 4.6 The Equation That Matters
docs.text:
You can now formalize it:

Effective IO = Ingestion IO × Amplification Factor

docs.title: 4.7 Why This Is Dangerous
docs.text:
This relationship is not obvious when you build the system.

Because:

  • You measure ingestion
  • You measure queries
  • But amplification is hidden

So your system appears:

  • Efficient at small scale
  • Unpredictable at large scale

docs.title: 4.8 Where Amplification Comes From
docs.text: Let’s unpack the drivers.

docs.title: 1. Part Size
docs.text:
From Chapter 3:

  • Smaller parts → more merge levels
  • More merge levels → more rewrites

docs.title: 2. Partition Fragmentation
docs.text:
If data is spread across many partitions:

  • Each partition merges independently
  • Fewer parts per partition
  • More merge levels

docs.title: 3. Continuous Ingestion
docs.text:
If new parts keep arriving:

  • Merge system never “catches up”
  • Lower-level merges dominate
  • Higher-level merges delayed

docs.title: 4. Merge Scheduling Heuristics
docs.text:
ClickHouse prefers:

  • Merging similar-sized parts
  • Avoiding very large merges

So:

  • Small parts get merged frequently
  • Large parts may be delayed

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text:
If small merges happen more often than large merges:

What happens to amplification?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Amplification increases.

Because data gets rewritten multiple times before reaching large size.

docs.title: 4.9 A Deeper Visualization
docs.text:
Think of data flowing through levels:

Insert → L0 → L1 → L2 → L3 → Final

Each arrow is a rewrite.

docs.title: Case A — Small Parts
docs.text:
Insert → L0 → L1 → L2 → L3 → L4 → Final

Many steps → high amplification

docs.title: Case B — Larger Parts
docs.text:
Insert → L0 → L1 → Final

Fewer steps → lower amplification

docs.title: 4.10 The Non-Linear Trap
docs.text:
Here’s the subtlety:

Amplification is not linear.

If you:

  • Reduce part size by 2×

You may:

  • Increase merge levels by more than 2×

Which means:

  • Amplification grows faster than expected

docs.title: 4.11 The IO Illusion
docs.text:
At this point, you might think:

“We just need more IO bandwidth.”

But pause.

docs.title: 🤔 Question
docs.text:
If you double IO capacity…

But amplification remains the same…

What happens in a few months as data grows?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
You hit the limit again.

Because:

  • Amplification is still multiplying your workload

docs.title: 4.12 Optimization vs Reality
docs.text: This leads to a crucial distinction.

docs.title: Stage 1 — Inefficient System
docs.text:
• Small parts
  • High amplification
  • IO inflated artificially

Fix:

  • Increase batch size
  • Reduce parts/sec

docs.title: Stage 2 — Efficient System
docs.text:
• Large parts
  • Minimal amplification
  • IO reflects actual data movement

At this point:

You are bound by physical limits.

docs.title: 4.13 A Concrete Comparison
docs.text: Let’s compare two systems.

docs.title: System A
docs.text:
• Ingestion: 600 MB/sec
  • Amplification: 5×
Effective IO = 3 GB/sec

docs.title: System B
docs.text:
• Ingestion: 600 MB/sec
  • Amplification: 2×
Effective IO = 1.2 GB/sec

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: Which system is more scalable?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
System B.

Because:

  • Lower amplification
  • Lower IO pressure
  • More headroom

docs.title: 4.14 The Critical Realization
docs.text:
You don’t scale ClickHouse by just handling more data.

You scale it by:

Reducing how many times that data is rewritten.

docs.title: 4.15 Stress Test
docs.text:
Suppose:

  • You increase batch size 10×
  • Parts become 10× larger

What happens to:

  • Merge levels?
  • Amplification?
  • IO?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
• Merge levels ↓
  • Amplification ↓
  • IO ↓

Even though:

  • Raw ingestion remains constant

docs.title: 4.16 The Dangerous Blind Spot
docs.text:
Many teams:

  • Monitor ingestion rate
  • Monitor query latency

But ignore:

Amplification

Which is why they say:

“System suddenly became unstable”

When in reality:

Amplification quietly increased over time

docs.title: 4.17 The Deep Mental Model
docs.text:
You can now extend your system equation:

Total IO = Ingestion IO × Amplification Factor + Query IO

And in many systems:

Amplification dominates.

docs.title: 4.18 Closing Insight
docs.text:
If you take one thing from this chapter:

Merge amplification is the invisible multiplier that turns a manageable system into an IO-bound system.

docs.title: 5.1 A System That Refuses to “Fix Itself”
docs.text:
Let’s revisit a familiar situation.

You have:

  • Continuous ingestion
  • Reasonable batching (not terrible)
  • Time-based partitioning
  • Enough hardware

Yet, over time, you observe:

  • Many small parts still exist
  • Large parts are forming… but slowly
  • Merge backlog is growing

You look at the system and think:

“Why doesn’t ClickHouse just merge all these small parts quickly and be done with it?”

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text:
If you had complete control, what would you do?

  • Merge everything aggressively?
  • Always prioritize largest merges?
  • Always clean up smallest parts first?

Hold that thought.

docs.title: 5.2 The Naive Strategy (And Why It Fails)
docs.text:
Let’s say you design a “perfect” merge strategy:

“Always merge as many parts as possible into one big part.”

Sounds ideal.

docs.title: What happens?
docs.text:
• Huge merges start
  • Each merge reads massive data
  • IO spikes
  • Queries slow down
  • System becomes unstable

So this strategy is not viable.

docs.title: 5.3 The Opposite Strategy
docs.text:
Now try the opposite:

“Only merge very small parts.”

docs.title: What happens?
docs.text:
• Small parts get merged into medium parts
  • But medium parts never get merged further
  • System accumulates mid-sized parts
  • Amplification still high

Again — not ideal.

docs.title: 5.4 The Reality: Heuristic Scheduling
docs.text:
ClickHouse does not use a globally optimal merge plan.

Instead, it uses heuristics.

At a high level:

  • Prefer merging parts of similar size
  • Avoid very large merges unless necessary
  • Keep merges incremental
  • Balance IO usage

This is practical — but not perfect.

docs.title: 5.5 The Merge Ladder (Revisited with Behavior)
docs.text:
Recall the levels:

L0 → L1 → L2 → L3 → L4

Now add behavior:

  • System prefers merging within same level
  • Progression to next level is gradual
  • Larger merges are rarer

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text:
If new small parts keep arriving continuously…

What happens to this ladder?

docs.title: 5.6 The Core Problem: Continuous Pressure
docs.text: Let’s walk through it slowly.

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text: New small parts arrive → L0 fills up

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text: Merge scheduler picks small parts → L1 formed

docs.title: Step 3
docs.text:
But before L1 can be merged further…

More L0 parts arrive

docs.title: 🤯 The Consequence
docs.text:
The system keeps doing:

L0 → L1 → L0 → L1 → L0 → L1

But struggles to do:

L1 → L2 → L3

docs.title: 💡 Insight
docs.text:
The system gets stuck in lower levels.

This is merge starvation.

docs.title: 5.7 What Is Starvation?
docs.text:
Merge starvation means:

Higher-level merges are delayed indefinitely because lower-level work never stops.

docs.title: 🤔 Think
docs.text:
Which merges are cheaper?

  • Small merges (L0 → L1)
  • Large merges (L2 → L3)

docs.title: Answer
docs.text: Small merges.

docs.title: 5.8 The Scheduler’s Bias
docs.text:
Because small merges:

  • Require less IO
  • Finish faster
  • Are safer

The scheduler tends to:

Keep picking small merges

docs.title: 🤯 The Paradox
docs.text:
This leads to a paradox:

The system keeps doing the “easy work”

and postpones the “important work”

docs.title: 5.9 The Resulting State
docs.text:
You end up with:

  • Many small and medium parts
  • Few large consolidated parts
  • High amplification
  • Persistent merge backlog

docs.title: 5.10 Why This Is Hard to See
docs.text:
From outside, the system looks active:

  • Merges are happening
  • CPU is doing work
  • IO is flowing

So it feels like:

“System is working hard”

But in reality:

It’s working on the wrong level of the problem.

docs.title: 5.11 A More Intuitive Analogy
docs.text:
Think of it like cleaning a warehouse.

  • New boxes arrive constantly
  • Workers keep organizing small boxes
  • But never get time to consolidate large sections

So the warehouse is:

  • Busy
  • Active
  • Still messy

docs.title: 5.12 The Feedback Loop
docs.text:
Let’s connect the dots.

  1. Small parts arrive continuously
  2. Scheduler prefers small merges
  3. Large merges delayed
  4. Amplification increases
  5. IO increases
  6. Merge speed decreases
  7. Backlog grows
  8. Even more pressure on small merges

This is a self-reinforcing loop.

docs.title: 5.13 The Hidden Trigger
docs.text:
Notice something important:

Starvation is not caused by lack of resources.

It is caused by:

The combination of continuous ingestion + merge heuristics

docs.title: 5.14 The Wrong Fix
docs.text:
At this point, many engineers try:

  • Increase merge threads
  • Increase CPU
  • Increase memory

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: Will this fix starvation?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Not necessarily.

Because:

  • More threads still follow same heuristic
  • IO remains the bottleneck
  • You may increase contention

docs.title: 5.15 The Correct Fix
docs.text:
To break starvation, you must:

Reduce pressure on lower levels

docs.title: How?
docs.text:
1. Increase batch size
    • Fewer small parts
    • Less L0 pressure
  2. Reduce parts/sec
    • Give system time to climb levels
  3. Improve merge efficiency
    • Larger initial parts

docs.title: 💡 Insight
docs.text:
You don’t fix starvation by speeding up merges.

You fix it by reducing the amount of small work entering the system.

docs.title: 5.16 A Subtle Observation
docs.text:
You might see:

  • Merges are happening
  • But part sizes not increasing significantly

That is a red flag.

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text:
If merges are happening but part sizes don’t grow…

What does that mean?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text: System is stuck in lower levels → starvation.

docs.title: 5.17 Connecting All Chapters
docs.text:
Now connect everything:

  • Chapter 2: parts/sec matters
  • Chapter 3: small parts increase levels
  • Chapter 4: more levels → amplification
  • Chapter 5: scheduler can get stuck in lower levels

docs.title: 5.18 Final Mental Model
docs.text:
The system is like:

Incoming parts → merge pipeline → final large parts

If input pressure is too high:

Pipeline never completes.

docs.title: 5.19 Closing Insight
docs.text:
If you remember one thing:

ClickHouse merge system is not globally optimal —

it is locally efficient and can get stuck under continuous pressure.

docs.title: 🔚 End of Chapter 5
docs.text:
Next:

👉 Chapter 6 — ORDER BY as a Physical Design Tool

We’ll shift gears slightly:

  • From writes and merges
  • To how data is physically laid out for reads

This is where your earlier ClickHouse intuition (city, time, rider) will connect deeply.

Before we proceed:

Do you want Chapter 6 to include:

  • Your earlier ride_events examples (city, driver, rider) 👉 This will make it very concrete

Or keep it generic?

docs.title: Order By - A Physical Design Tool
6.1 The Table You Designed
docs.text:
Let’s say you’re designing a core table:

ride_events(
    request_id,
    rider_id,
    driver_id,
    city_id,
    request_time,
    fare,
    status
)

This table powers:

  • Dashboards (time-based trends)
  • City-level analysis
  • Driver performance queries
  • Rider lookups (occasionally)

You now need to define:

ORDERBY ( ? )

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text:
What would you choose?

Don’t rush — this is one of the most important decisions in ClickHouse.

docs.title: 6.2 The First Instinct
docs.text:
A common instinct is:

“Let’s include the most important fields”

So you might write:

ORDERBY (rider_id, driver_id, city_id, request_time)

Or even:

ORDERBY (request_time, city_id, driver_id, rider_id)

Feels safe.

Feels flexible.

docs.title: ❌ The Hidden Assumption
docs.text:
This assumes:

ORDER BY behaves like a multi-column index in OLTP systems.

But it doesn’t.

docs.title: 6.3 What ORDER BY Actually Does
docs.text:
In ClickHouse, ORDER BY defines:

The physical layout of data on disk

When data is written:

  • Rows are sorted by ORDER BY
  • Stored in that order
  • Granules follow this order
  • Index reflects this order

So:

ORDER BY is not an index.

It is how your data is physically arranged.

docs.title: 6.4 The Prefix Rule (Revisited Deeply)
docs.text:
Let’s say you choose:

ORDERBY (request_time, city_id)

Data is physically grouped like:

time1 → cityA
time1 → cityB
time2 → cityA
time2 → cityB
...

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text:
Now consider this query:

WHERE request_timeBETWEEN XAND Y

Efficient or not?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Very efficient.

Because:

  • Data is contiguous in time
  • Binary search on primary index works well
  • Few granules read

docs.title: 6.5 Now Change the Query
docs.text: WHERE city_id=5

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: Efficient or not?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Not efficient.

Because:

  • city_id is not leading key
  • Data is scattered across time
  • Many granules must be scanned

docs.title: 💡 Insight
docs.text: ORDER BY only helps if your filter aligns with its prefix

docs.title: 6.6 Let’s Flip the Design
docs.text:
Now try:

ORDERBY (city_id, request_time)

Data looks like:

cityA → time1, time2, time3...
cityB → time1, time2, time3...

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: Now evaluate:

docs.title: Query 1
docs.text: WHERE city_id=5AND request_timeBETWEEN XAND Y

docs.title: Query 2
docs.text: WHERE request_timeBETWEEN XAND Y

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
Query 1 → very efficient

Query 2 → less efficient

docs.title: 6.7 The Real Tradeoff
docs.text:
You cannot optimize for everything.

You must choose:

Which queries deserve physical locality?

docs.title: 6.8 Your Workload (Ride Events)
docs.text:
Let’s say your workload is:

  • 60% → time-only queries
  • 25% → city + time
  • 10% → driver + time
  • 5% → rider lookups

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: Which ORDER BY would you choose?

docs.title: 6.9 The Tempting Answer
docs.text:
You might think:

“City has skew (top 3 cities = 70% traffic), so let’s use city first” 

ORDERBY (city_id, request_time)

docs.title: ❌ Why This Is Risky
docs.text: Let’s analyze.

docs.title: Compression Argument
docs.text:
Yes:

  • City clustering improves RLE
  • High skew helps compression

But:

docs.title: Time Column Behavior
docs.text:
With:

ORDERBY (city_id, request_time)

Time becomes:

  • Non-monotonic globally
  • Reset within each city

This hurts:

  • Delta encoding
  • Compression
  • Merge efficiency

docs.title: 🤯 Hidden Cost
docs.text:
You optimized one column (city),

but degraded another (time) — often a larger column.

docs.title: 6.10 The Correct Reasoning
docs.text:
Given workload:

  • 60% queries are time-based
  • Data arrives time-ordered

Best choice:

ORDERBY (request_time, city_id)

docs.title: 💡 Insight
docs.text: Optimize for the dimension that dominates data scanned, not just frequency.

docs.title: 6.11 What About Driver Queries?
docs.text:
Query:

WHERE driver_id= XAND request_timeBETWEEN ...

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: Will ORDER BY help?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Not much.

Because:

  • driver_id not in prefix
  • data scattered

docs.title: 6.12 The Realization
docs.text:
ORDER BY cannot serve all access patterns.

So what do you do?

docs.title: 6.13 The Options
docs.text:
For driver queries:

  1. Accept slower performance
  2. Use projections
  3. Use pre-aggregated tables
  4. Use skipping indexes

This introduces a layered design (we’ll revisit later).

docs.title: 6.14 A Subtle but Critical Insight
docs.text:
ORDER BY also affects:

  • Merge efficiency
  • Compression
  • Insert cost

Not just queries.

docs.title: 🤔 Think
docs.text:
If data arrives sorted by time…

And ORDER BY starts with time…

What happens during insert?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text: Minimal reshuffling → efficient ingestion.

docs.title: 6.15 If You Misalign ORDER BY
docs.text:
Example:

ORDERBY (city_id, request_time)

But data arrives time-ordered.

Now:

  • Insert must reshuffle data
  • Merge cost increases
  • CPU increases

docs.title: 💡 Insight
docs.text: Good ORDER BY aligns with both query patterns and ingestion order

docs.title: 6.16 The Prefix Law (Final Form)
docs.text:
For:

ORDERBY (A, B, C)

You get strong pruning only when:

  • A is filtered
  • A + B are filtered

Everything else is degraded.

docs.title: 6.17 Stress Test
docs.text:
Suppose you choose:

ORDERBY (request_time, city_id)

Now consider:

WHERE city_id=5AND request_timeBETWEEN ...

Efficient?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Yes — because:

  • request_time prunes first
  • city_id refines within range

docs.title: 6.18 Final Mental Model
docs.text:
ORDER BY defines:

Physical clustering → Index structure → Compression → Merge behavior

docs.title: 6.19 Closing Insight
docs.text:
If you remember one thing:

ORDER BY is not a query optimization hint.

It is the physical shape of your data on disk.

docs.title: Granules, Primary Index, and the Illusion of Skipping
7.1 A Query That “Should Be Fast”
docs.text:
Let’s go back to your ride_events table:

ORDERBY (request_time, city_id)

Now consider this query:

SELECT*
FROM ride_events
WHERE rider_id=123456

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text:
Your intuition might say:

“We have an index, so it should be fast.”

But we already know:

  • rider_id is not in ORDER BY prefix
  • So primary index won’t help much

So you think:

“Let’s add a bloom filter index.” 

INDEX rider_bf rider_id TYPE bloom_filter(0.01)

Now ask:

Will this query be fast?

docs.title: 7.2 The Comfortable but Wrong Mental Model
docs.text:
Most people think:

“Index → jump directly to data”

That’s true in OLTP systems.

But ClickHouse is not doing:

  • Row-level indexing
  • Pointer chasing

Instead, it works in blocks (granules).

docs.title: 7.3 What Is a Granule (Precisely)
docs.text:
Inside each part:

  • Data is sorted by ORDER BY
  • Then divided into chunks of:
index_granularity ≈ 8192 rows

Each granule:

  • Contains ~8192 rows
  • Is the smallest unit of data skipping

docs.title: 7.4 What the Primary Index Stores
docs.text:
For each granule:

  • Store the first ORDER BY key

Example:

Granule 1 → (time=10:00, city=1)
Granule 2 → (time=10:05, city=2)
Granule 3 → (time=10:10, city=1)
...

This means:

Primary index is sparse and prefix-based

docs.title: 7.5 How Query Execution Actually Works
docs.text: Let’s trace the flow.

docs.title: Step 1 — Partition Pruning
docs.text: Skip partitions based on partition key.

docs.title: Step 2 — Part Selection
docs.text: Each part is considered independently.

docs.title: Step 3 — Primary Index Pruning
docs.text: Binary search on ORDER BY prefix only

docs.title: Step 4 — Granule Filtering
docs.text: Selected granules are read.

docs.title: Step 5 — Actual Filtering
docs.text: Row-level filtering happens after reading.

docs.title: 💡 Critical Insight
docs.text: ClickHouse skips granules, not rows.

docs.title: 7.6 Now Let’s Analyze rider_id Query
docs.text:
We have:

  • rider_id not in ORDER BY
  • Uniform distribution

So:

  • Primary index cannot prune
  • Every granule is a candidate

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: How many granules are we talking about?

docs.title: 7.7 Let’s Do the Math
docs.text:
Assume:

  • Total rows = 10 billion
  • Granule size = 8192

Number of granules:

10,000,000,000 / 8192 ≈ 1.2 million granules

Now:

Each granule has ~8192 rows.

Total distinct riders:

~200 million riders

So expected riders per granule:

8192 / 200,000,000 ≈ 0.004%

Very sparse.

docs.title: 7.8 Now Add Bloom Filter
docs.text:
For each granule:

  • Bloom filter checks if rider might exist

Let’s say query:

WHERE rider_idIN (1000 riders)

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: What fraction of granules will pass the bloom filter?

docs.title: 7.9 The Probability Calculation
docs.text:
Probability a given rider exists in a granule:

p = 8192 / 200,000,000 ≈ 0.00004

For 1000 riders:

Probability at least one exists:

P = 1 - e^(-1000 × p)
  ≈ 1 - e^(-0.04)
  ≈ 4%

docs.title: 7.10 What Does That Mean?
docs.text:
Out of:

1.2 million granules

We scan:

~4% ≈ 48,000 granules

Rows scanned:

48,000 × 8192 ≈ 400 million rows

docs.title: 🤯 Reality Check
docs.text:
You asked for 1000 riders.

But you scanned 400 million rows.

docs.title: 💡 Insight
docs.text: Bloom filters reduce IO probabilistically — but cannot eliminate it.

docs.title: 7.11 Why This Happens
docs.text:
Because:

  • Bloom filter works per granule
  • Granules contain multiple values
  • IN queries increase probability of match

docs.title: 7.12 The Illusion of Skipping
docs.text:
At a high level:

  • You feel like you’re “filtering data”
  • But you’re actually filtering granules probabilistically

docs.title: 7.13 Now Compare With Projection
docs.text:
If you had:

PROJECTION (rider_id, request_time)

Data physically sorted by rider_id.

Now:

  • Binary search per rider
  • Very few granules read

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: What is the difference?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Projection gives:

Deterministic pruning

Bloom filter gives:

Probabilistic pruning

docs.title: 7.14 Granule Size Tradeoff (Deep Dive)
docs.text:
Recall:

default = 8192 rows

docs.title: If you reduce to 2048:
docs.text:
Pros:

  • Smaller granules
  • Better skipping precision

Cons:

  • 4× more granules
  • 4× larger primary index
  • More metadata scans

docs.title: 🤔 Think
docs.text: Does this reduce bloom filter scanning?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text: Yes — but increases metadata cost.

docs.title: 7.15 Another Subtlety
docs.text:
Granules are not stored independently.

So:

  • Even if you skip many granules
  • You still pay cost for:
    • Index scanning
    • Metadata traversal

docs.title: 7.16 Why Primary Index Is Powerful (When Used Correctly)
docs.text:
If query matches ORDER BY prefix:

Example:

WHERE request_timeBETWEEN XAND Y

Then:

  • Binary search finds exact granules
  • No probabilistic scanning
  • Minimal IO

docs.title: 💡 Insight
docs.text:
Primary index is exact but limited

Bloom filter is flexible but approximate

docs.title: 7.17 The Cardinality Trap
docs.text:
You earlier asked:

“Riders have low activity — does bloom help?”

Now you see:

  • High cardinality helps
  • But uniform distribution hurts

Because:

  • Values spread across granules
  • Hard to isolate

docs.title: 7.18 Final Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of ClickHouse as:

Granule-level system, not row-level system

All skipping decisions happen at granule level.

docs.title: 7.19 Closing Insight
docs.text:
If you remember one thing:

ClickHouse does not jump to rows —

it narrows down to granules and then scans within them.

docs.title: IO Vs CPU - Finding The Real Bottleneck
8.1 A Pager Goes Off
docs.text:
It’s a regular day.

Suddenly, alerts fire:

  • Query latency ↑
  • Dashboard slow
  • Some timeouts

You open metrics:

  • CPU ~40%
  • Memory fine
  • But IO is high

At first glance, it’s confusing.

“CPU is not maxed… so why is the system slow?”

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: What is your first instinct?

docs.title: 8.2 The First Mistake
docs.text:
A common reaction:

“Let’s increase threads / CPU”

Because:

  • CPU is underutilized
  • More parallelism should help

docs.title: ❌ Why This Can Backfire
docs.text:
If the system is IO-bound:

  • More threads → more concurrent IO
  • More contention
  • Higher latency per operation

You end up:

Slowing the system further

docs.title: 8.3 The Fundamental Question
docs.text:
Before doing anything, you must answer:

Is the system CPU-bound or IO-bound?

docs.title: 8.4 How to Think About This
docs.text: Let’s simplify:

docs.title: CPU-bound system
docs.text:
• CPU ~90–100%
  • IO moderate
  • Threads busy

docs.title: IO-bound system
docs.text:
• CPU low/moderate
  • IO saturated
  • Threads waiting

docs.title: 💡 Insight
docs.text: Low CPU + high latency usually means IO bottleneck.

docs.title: 8.5 But “IO High” Is Not Enough
docs.text:
Here’s where many engineers stop.

They say:

“IO is high → that’s the problem”

But that’s incomplete.

You need to ask:

Why is IO high?

docs.title: 8.6 Two Very Different IO Problems
docs.text: There are two fundamentally different scenarios.

docs.title: Case 1 — Amplification Problem
docs.text:
• Many small parts
  • High parts/sec
  • Merge backlog growing

IO is high because:

System is rewriting data too many times

docs.title: Case 2 — Absolute Throughput Problem
docs.text:
• Parts already large
  • parts/sec low
  • Merge backlog still present

IO is high because:

System is processing too much data overall

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: Why is this distinction important?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Because:

The fixes are completely different.

docs.title: 8.7 Real-World Debugging Flow
docs.text: Now let’s walk through how a expert would debug this.

docs.title: Step 1 — Look at Parts
docs.text:
Ask:

  • How many active parts exist?
  • Is the number growing?

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• Many small parts → amplification problem
  • Few large parts → volume problem

docs.title: Step 2 — Check Part Sizes
docs.text:
Ask:

  • Average part size?

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• Very small parts → batching issue
  • Healthy sizes (~100MB+) → look elsewhere

docs.title: Step 3 — Observe Merge Backlog
docs.text:
Ask:

  • Are merges lagging behind?

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• Yes → merge system overloaded
  • No → problem elsewhere (queries?)

docs.title: Step 4 — Check CPU vs IO
docs.text:
Ask:

  • CPU utilization?
  • IO throughput?

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: CPU IO Meaning High Moderate CPU-bound Low High IO-bound

docs.title: Step 5 — Correlate with Ingestion
docs.text:
Ask:

  • Did ingestion pattern change?
  • Smaller batches?
  • Higher frequency?

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: • Yes → parts/sec increased → amplification

docs.title: Step 6 — Look at Query Patterns
docs.text:
Ask:

  • Are queries scanning more data?
  • Different filters?

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: • New queries → scan-heavy → IO increase

docs.title: 8.8 Putting It Together
docs.text: You now classify:

docs.title: Scenario A
docs.text:
• Small parts
  • High parts/sec
  • Merge backlog

👉 Root cause: Amplification

Fix:

  • Increase batch size
  • Reduce parts/sec

docs.title: Scenario B
docs.text:
• Large parts
  • Low parts/sec
  • IO saturated

👉 Root cause: Absolute volume

Fix:

  • Pre-aggregation
  • Reduce data scanned
  • Increase IO capacity

docs.title: 8.9 The Dangerous Misdiagnosis
docs.text: If you confuse the two:

docs.title: Treat amplification as volume
docs.text:
You:

  • Add hardware
  • Increase IO

Result:

  • Temporary relief
  • Problem returns

docs.title: Treat volume as amplification
docs.text:
You:

  • Increase batch size

Result:

  • No meaningful improvement

docs.title: 8.10 A Real Example
docs.text: Let’s simulate.

docs.title: System State
docs.text:
• Parts size: 50k rows
  • Parts/sec: high
  • IO: 3GB/sec
  • CPU: 30%

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: What is the problem?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text: Amplification.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
• Increase batch size
  • Reduce parts/sec

docs.title: Another System
docs.text:
• Parts size: 200MB
  • Parts/sec: low
  • IO: 3GB/sec
  • CPU: 30%

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: Now what?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text: Absolute throughput limit.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
• Pre-aggregate
  • Reduce data volume

docs.title: 8.11 Why CPU Can Be Low
docs.text:
This is counterintuitive.

You might think:

“System is slow → CPU should be high”

But in IO-bound systems:

  • Threads wait on IO
  • CPU stays idle

docs.title: 💡 Insight
docs.text: Low CPU is often a sign of a blocked system, not an idle one.

docs.title: 8.12 The Role of Object Storage
docs.text:
In cloud setups:

  • IO includes network latency
  • Object store throughput limits
  • Request overhead

So IO bottlenecks are even more pronounced.

docs.title: 8.13 The Debugging Mindset
docs.text:
You:

  1. Identify bottleneck (CPU vs IO)
  2. Identify cause (amplification vs volume)
  3. Apply correct lever

docs.title: 8.14 The Decision Tree
docs.text:
Slow system
→ CPU high? → optimize compute
→ CPU low, IO high?
      → small parts? → fix batching
      → large parts? → reduce volume

docs.title: 8.15 Closing Insight
docs.text:
If you remember one thing:

The hardest part of scaling ClickHouse is not tuning —

it is correctly identifying whether you are IO-bound due to amplification or absolute data volume.

docs.title: 9.1 A System That Is “Well-Tuned”… Yet Failing
docs.text:
Let’s construct a system that you would be proud of.

  • Batch size optimized
  • Parts are large (~200MB)
  • Merge amplification under control
  • ORDER BY aligned with workload
  • Partitioning reasonable
  • Queries optimized

You’ve done everything right.

Yet, over time:

  • IO is constantly saturated
  • Merge backlog exists (but not exploding)
  • Query latency slowly degrades
  • Scaling hardware helps… temporarily

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text:
If everything is optimized…

Why is the system still struggling?

docs.title: 9.2 The First Reaction
docs.text:
A natural response:

“We need more IO bandwidth”

So you:

  • Upgrade storage tier
  • Increase network bandwidth
  • Add more nodes

And yes — things improve.

For a while.

Then the problem returns.

docs.title: 9.3 The Uncomfortable Realization
docs.text:
At this point, you’re forced to confront something deeper:

The system is not inefficient.

The system is too large.

docs.title: 9.4 Reframing the Problem
docs.text:
Up to now, your focus was:

“How efficiently can we process this data?”

Now the question becomes:

“Should we even be processing this much data?”

docs.title: 9.5 The Two Phases of Scaling
docs.text: Let’s define two distinct phases.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Optimization Phase
docs.text:
• System inefficient
  • Amplification high
  • Small parts
  • Fixable with tuning

docs.title: Phase 2 — Saturation Phase
docs.text:
• System efficient
  • Amplification minimal
  • Parts large
  • IO still saturated

You are now in Phase 2.

docs.title: 💡 Insight
docs.text:
Optimization reduces inefficiency.

It does not eliminate scale.

docs.title: 9.6 The Physics Limit
docs.text:
At this stage:

Total IO ≈ Actual data movement

No hidden multiplier.

No inefficiency.

Just:

Bytes in → bytes processed → bytes out

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text:
If IO is saturated even in this state…

What does that imply?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text: You’ve hit the physical throughput limit of the system.

docs.title: 9.7 The Cost Dimension Enters
docs.text:
Until now, you were thinking technically.

Now introduce cost.

docs.title: Assume
docs.text:
• Object storage: ₹2–3 per GB/month
  • IO bandwidth: charged per TB
  • Compute: per node/hour

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Your system processes:

5 TB per hour

Even with perfect efficiency:

  • Storage cost scales linearly
  • IO cost scales linearly
  • Compute cost scales linearly

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text:
If your data grows 10×…

What happens to cost?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text: Cost grows 10×.

docs.title: 9.8 The Core Problem
docs.text:
Scaling via hardware means:

You are chasing growth with linear cost.

At PB scale, this becomes:

  • Financially unsustainable
  • Operationally fragile

docs.title: 9.9 The Only Real Lever Left
docs.text:
At this point, one option remains:

Reduce the amount of data you process.

docs.title: 9.10 Enter Pre-Aggregation
docs.text:
Instead of storing:

  • Every event

You store:

  • Aggregated summaries

Example:

Instead of:

1 row per ride

Store:

1 row per (city, hour)

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: What happens to data volume?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Massive reduction.

Possibly:

  • 10×
  • 100×
  • Even 1000×

docs.title: 9.11 The Immediate Impact
docs.text:
Reducing data volume affects everything:

  • IO ↓
  • Storage ↓
  • Merge workload ↓
  • Query latency ↓

docs.title: 9.12 The Deeper Impact
docs.text:
More importantly:

You change the growth curve of the system.

docs.title: Without Pre-Aggregation
docs.text:
Data(t) = k × t

Linear growth.

docs.title: With Pre-Aggregation
docs.text:
Data(t) = (k × t) / reduction_factor

Lower slope.

docs.title: 9.13 Why Hardware Scaling Fails Long-Term
docs.text: Let’s compare.

docs.title: Option A — Scale Hardware
docs.text:
• Increase IO bandwidth
  • Add nodes

Result:

  • Linear cost increase
  • Temporary relief

docs.title: Option B — Reduce Data Volume
docs.text:
• Pre-aggregation
  • Smarter modeling

Result:

  • Permanent cost reduction
  • Sustainable scaling

docs.title: 💡 Insight
docs.text: At scale, reducing data movement is more powerful than increasing system capacity.

docs.title: 9.14 The Tradeoff You Must Accept
docs.text: Pre-aggregation is not free.

docs.title: Costs
docs.text:
• More complex pipelines
  • Upstream computation (Spark, Flink)
  • Reduced flexibility (less raw detail)
  • Backfill complexity

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: So why is it still worth it?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Because:

It trades operational instability and cost explosion

for controlled complexity.

docs.title: 9.15 A Subtle Decision Point
docs.text:
You must ask:

Is this workload fundamentally analytical?

If yes:

  • Pre-aggregation is natural

If no:

  • You may need hybrid architecture

docs.title: 9.16 A Real Decision Framework
docs.text: At this stage, your choices become architectural:

docs.title: Option 1 — Keep Raw Only
docs.text:
• Flexible
  • Expensive
  • Hard to scale

docs.title: Option 2 — Raw + Aggregated
docs.text:
• Balanced
  • Common approach
  • More complexity

docs.title: Option 3 — Aggregation-First
docs.text:
• Highly scalable
  • Lowest cost
  • Limited flexibility

docs.title: 9.17 The expert-Level Shift
docs.text:
Earlier, you asked:

“How do I optimize this system?”

Now you ask:

“What should this system even be responsible for?”

docs.title: 9.18 The Boundary of ClickHouse
docs.text:
ClickHouse is excellent at:

  • Aggregations
  • Scans
  • Compression

But:

It should not be forced to solve problems better handled upstream.

docs.title: 9.19 Final Mental Model
docs.text:
System scaling evolves like:

Fix inefficiency → Hit limits → Change architecture

docs.title: 9.20 Closing Insight
docs.text:
If you remember one thing:

Optimization buys time.

Architecture buys scalability.

I’d strongly recommend the second.

docs.title: 10.1 The Problem Statement
docs.text:
You are building a platform like Uber.

Data:

  • Every ride generates events
  • Millions of events per second
  • Global scale
  • Multiple cities, drivers, riders

Use cases:

  • Real-time dashboards (rides per city, hour)
  • Driver performance
  • Surge pricing analytics
  • Rider behavior (limited)
  • Internal analytics

At first, it seems simple:

“Let’s dump everything into ClickHouse and query it.”

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text:
Based on everything you’ve learned so far…

What could go wrong?

docs.title: 10.2 The Naive Architecture
docs.text:
Let’s write it explicitly.

Producers → Kafka → ClickHouse (raw table) → Queries

Single table:

ride_eventsORDERBY (request_time, city_id)

docs.title: Why this feels right
docs.text:
• Simple
  • Flexible
  • All data in one place

docs.title: What happens over time
docs.text:
• Data grows to TB → PB
  • Queries scan massive data
  • Merge IO explodes
  • System becomes IO-bound
  • Costs increase rapidly

docs.title: 💡 Insight
docs.text: Simplicity at small scale becomes fragility at large scale.

docs.title: 10.3 The First Evolution — Aggregation
docs.text:
You introduce:

Raw Table → Aggregated Table

Example:

city_hourly_metrics
(
    city_id,
hour,
    ride_count,
    avg_fare
)

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: What changes?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
• Queries now hit smaller tables
  • Less data scanned
  • Lower IO
  • Better latency

But raw table still exists.

docs.title: 10.4 The Second Problem — Multi-Tenancy
docs.text:
Now introduce tenants:

  • Different business units
  • Or external clients
  • Or geographies

Assume:

  • 500 tenants
  • Top 5 tenants generate 60% of traffic

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: Should all tenants share the same table?

docs.title: 10.5 The Naive Answer
docs.text:
“Yes — just add tenant_id” 

ORDERBY (request_time, city_id, tenant_id)

docs.title: ❌ Why This Fails
docs.text:
• tenant_id increases cardinality
  • Breaks clustering
  • Merge efficiency drops
  • Large tenants dominate merges
  • Small tenants suffer

docs.title: 💡 Insight
docs.text: Logical isolation is not the same as physical isolation.

docs.title: 10.6 The Correct Strategy — Workload Isolation
docs.text:
Instead of:

One table for all

You design:

docs.title: Large Tenants
docs.text:
• Dedicated tables
  • Possibly dedicated clusters

docs.title: Small Tenants
docs.text: • Shared table

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: Why isolate only large tenants?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Because:

Workload is skewed, not uniform.

docs.title: 10.7 The Architecture Evolves
docs.text:
Now your system looks like:

                ┌───────────────┐
                │ Kafka Stream  │
                └──────┬────────┘
                       │
        ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
        │              │              │
   Large Tenant   Large Tenant   Small Tenants
      Pipeline        Pipeline        Pipeline
        │              │              │
        ▼              ▼              ▼
   CH Table A     CH Table B     Shared Table
        │              │              │
        └──────┬───────┴───────┬──────┘
               ▼               ▼
        Aggregated Tables (per segment)

docs.title: 10.8 Where Pre-Aggregation Fits
docs.text: Pre-aggregation can happen:

docs.title: Option 1 — Inside ClickHouse
docs.text:
• Materialized views
  • Simple but still IO heavy

docs.title: Option 2 — Upstream (Recommended)
docs.text:
• Spark / Flink jobs
  • Write aggregated data directly

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: Why prefer upstream?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Because:

You reduce data before it hits ClickHouse

→ reduces merges

→ reduces IO

docs.title: 10.9 The Aggregation-First Philosophy
docs.text: At scale, you shift mindset:

docs.title: Old
docs.text: Raw table is the source of truth for all queries

docs.title: New
docs.text:
Aggregated tables are the primary query layer

Raw table is fallback / audit

docs.title: 💡 Insight
docs.text:
Raw data is for completeness

Aggregated data is for usability

docs.title: 10.10 Query Routing Layer
docs.text:
Now introduce another layer:

User Query → Router → Aggregated / Raw

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
• Dashboard → aggregated table
  • Ad-hoc → raw table
  • Heavy queries → restricted

docs.title: 10.11 Protecting the System
docs.text:
You enforce:

  • Query limits on raw tables
  • Rate limiting
  • Sandbox environments

docs.title: 🤔 Pause
docs.text: Why restrict raw queries?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
Because:

Raw queries can bypass all optimizations and break the system.

docs.title: 10.12 Storage Strategy
docs.text: Now think in tiers:

docs.title: Hot Data
docs.text:
• Recent days
  • High query frequency
  • Stored in ClickHouse

docs.title: Cold Data
docs.text:
• Historical
  • Rarely accessed
  • Stored in cheaper storage

docs.title: 10.13 Merge Pressure Control
docs.text:
With this architecture:

  • Raw ingestion reduced (due to aggregation)
  • Parts/sec reduced
  • Merge amplification reduced

docs.title: 10.14 Putting It All Together
docs.text: Let’s trace a full flow.

docs.title: Step 1 — Event Generation
docs.text: • Ride events generated

docs.title: Step 2 — Streaming Layer
docs.text: • Kafka buffers data

docs.title: Step 3 — Processing Layer
docs.text:
• Flink/Spark aggregates data
  • Produces:
    • Raw stream (optional)
    • Aggregated stream

docs.title: Step 4 — Storage Layer
docs.text:
• Raw → ClickHouse raw tables
  • Aggregated → ClickHouse aggregated tables

docs.title: Step 5 — Query Layer
docs.text:
• Most queries → aggregated tables
  • Rare queries → raw tables

docs.title: Step 6 — Isolation Layer
docs.text:
• Large tenants separated
  • Small tenants pooled

docs.title: 10.15 What You Achieve
docs.text:
• IO under control
  • Merge pressure manageable
  • Query latency predictable
  • Cost sustainable
  • System scalable

docs.title: 10.16 What You Avoid
docs.text:
• Part explosion
  • Merge starvation
  • Amplification runaway
  • IO collapse
  • Cost explosion

docs.title: 10.17 The Final Mental Model
docs.text:
You are no longer designing:

A database schema

You are designing:

A data processing system with controlled data movement

docs.title: 10.18 The Ultimate Insight
docs.text:
If you remember one thing:

The goal is not to make ClickHouse handle more data.

The goal is to ensure ClickHouse only sees the data it should handle

docs.title: Why This Chapter?
docs.text:
Modern data platforms are built by combining multiple technologies.

For example, a Spark job may read data stored as Parquet files from an Apache Iceberg table registered in a Hive Metastore, orchestrated by Airflow, and stored on Amazon S3.

For someone new to the ecosystem, this can be confusing.

Questions naturally arise:

  • Why do we need both Parquet and Iceberg?
  • Doesn't Parquet already store metadata?
  • If Hive already manages tables, why was Iceberg invented?
  • Which technology is responsible for what?

These questions cannot be answered by studying each technology in isolation.

Instead, we need to understand how the modern data lake evolved over time.

docs.title: The Journey
docs.text:
Throughout this section, we will follow the evolution of analytical storage technologies.

CSV
    ↓
Parquet
    ↓
Hive Tables
    ↓
Apache Iceberg

Each generation solved a different problem introduced by the previous one.

Rather than treating these as competing technologies, we will learn how they complement each other.

docs.title: Our Learning Philosophy
docs.text: For every technology, we will answer the same four questions.

docs.title: 1. Why was it invented?
docs.text: What problem did the industry face?

docs.title: 2. What does it solve?
docs.text: What responsibilities belong to this technology?

docs.title: 3. What does it not solve?
docs.text:
What responsibilities belong somewhere else?

Understanding these boundaries is just as important as understanding the technology itself.

docs.title: 4. Why did the industry move to the next generation?
docs.text:
Every technology has limitations.

Those limitations often become the motivation for the next generation of tools.

docs.title: A Guiding Principle
docs.text:
One idea will appear repeatedly throughout this journey.

Every technology has a primary responsibility.

For example:

Technology Primary Responsibility CSV Store tabular data Parquet Efficiently store analytical data in a file Hive Metastore Organize files into tables Apache Iceberg Manage the lifecycle of tables

Notice that these technologies do not replace one another.

Instead, they build upon one another.

An Iceberg table typically stores its data in Parquet files.

Understanding where one technology ends and the next begins is the key to understanding modern lakehouse architectures.

docs.title: What's Next?
docs.text:
Our first stop is one of the oldest data storage formats still in use today.

Before we understand why Parquet became the standard for analytical storage, we first need to understand the limitations of storing data in simple row-oriented text files such as CSV.

docs.title: Why This Chapter?
docs.text:
In the previous chapter, we saw that Parquet became the de facto storage format for analytical workloads.

However, before understanding Parquet, we first need to understand one of the most important design decisions in analytical storage:

Should data be stored row by row or column by column?

The answer depends entirely on the type of workload.

docs.title: Two Types of Workloads
docs.text: Most database workloads fall into one of two categories.

docs.title: Transactional (OLTP)
docs.text:
Examples:

  • Banking transactions
  • Online shopping
  • User registration
  • Updating customer information

Typical query:

SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE user_id = 101;

Here we want all information for one user.

docs.title: Analytical (OLAP)
docs.text:
Examples:

  • Total sales by country
  • Average order value
  • Most viewed products
  • Monthly revenue trends

Typical query:

SELECT AVG(price)
FROM sales
WHERE country = 'IN';

Here we want one or two columns across millions of rows.

This difference is the key motivation behind columnar storage.

docs.title: Row-Oriented Storage
docs.text:
Imagine a table:

user_id country age salary 101 IN 25 50000 102 US 30 70000 103 UK 28 60000

A row-oriented file stores data like this:

101,IN,25,50000
102,US,30,70000
103,UK,28,60000

Each row is stored together.

docs.title: Advantages of Row Storage
docs.text:
Reading a complete record is extremely efficient.

For example:

SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE user_id = 101;

Once the row is located, every column is already stored together.

Very little disk I/O is required.

This makes row-oriented storage ideal for transactional systems.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Now consider an analytical query:

SELECT AVG(salary)
FROM users;

We only need one column:

salary

However, with row-oriented storage, the database must repeatedly read:

user_id
country
age
salary

for every row.

Even though three of those columns are never used.

Most of the disk I/O is wasted.

docs.title: Column-Oriented Storage
docs.text:
Instead of storing rows together, column-oriented storage stores each column independently.

The same table becomes:

user_id

101
102
103

country

IN
US
UK

age

25
30
28

salary

50000
70000
60000

Now our analytical query:

SELECT AVG(salary)
FROM users;

only needs to read:

salary

The remaining columns are never touched.

This technique is called column pruning.

docs.title: Why This Is Faster
docs.text:
Suppose our table contains twenty columns.

customer_id
name
email
phone
address
country
...
salary
...

If our query only requires:

AVG(salary)

then nineteen columns can be skipped entirely.

Less data is read from disk.

Less data is transferred over the network.

Less memory is consumed.

Less CPU is required.

For analytical workloads involving billions of rows, these savings are enormous.

docs.title: Better Compression
docs.text:
Column-oriented storage provides another important advantage.

Consider the country column:

IN
IN
IN
IN
IN
IN
US
US
US
UK

Since similar values are stored together, compression algorithms become much more effective.

In contrast, row-oriented storage mixes many unrelated values together:

101,IN,25,50000
102,US,30,70000
103,UK,28,60000

Repeated values are scattered throughout the file, making compression less efficient.

docs.title: Does This Mean Row Storage Is Bad?
docs.text:
Not at all.

Each storage model is optimized for a different workload.

Row Storage Column Storage Read complete records Read selected columns OLTP workloads OLAP workloads Frequent updates Large analytical scans Point lookups Aggregations Transaction processing Business intelligence

Neither approach is universally better.

Choosing the wrong storage model for the workload leads to poor performance.

docs.title: What We Learned
docs.text:
Column-oriented storage was invented because analytical queries usually access a small subset of columns across a very large number of rows.

By storing each column independently, analytical systems can:

  • Read significantly less data
  • Compress data more efficiently
  • Reduce disk I/O
  • Improve query performance

This simple design decision became the foundation for modern analytical file formats such as Apache Parquet.

docs.title: What's Next?
docs.text:
Now that we understand why columnar storage is faster for analytics, we are ready to open the black box.

In the next chapter, we will look inside a Parquet file and understand how it stores data using row groups, column chunks, pages, and metadata.

docs.title: Why This Chapter?
docs.text:
In the previous chapter, we learned why column-oriented storage is well suited for analytical workloads.

Now it's time to look inside a Parquet file.

Although a Parquet file appears as a single binary file on disk, it has a carefully designed internal structure that allows query engines like Spark to efficiently locate metadata and read only the data they need.

This chapter focuses on one question:

How is a Parquet file physically organized?

docs.title: Conceptual Structure
docs.text:
At the highest level, every Parquet file consists of two logical parts.

+----------------------------------+
|                                  |
|             Data                 |
|                                  |
|        (Multiple Row Groups)     |
|                                  |
+----------------------------------+
|                                  |
|             Footer               |
|                                  |
+----------------------------------+

The Data section stores the actual records.

The Footer stores metadata describing how to interpret the data.

Notice that a Parquet file knows nothing about tables, partitions, snapshots, or transactions.

Its responsibility is simply to store one dataset efficiently.

docs.title: Magic Bytes
docs.text:
Every Parquet file begins and ends with the four-byte signature:

PAR1

These magic bytes allow readers to quickly verify that the file is indeed a valid Parquet file.

Think of them as the file's signature.

docs.title: Data Section
docs.text:
The majority of the file contains the actual data.

Rather than storing all rows together, the data is divided into multiple Row Groups.

Each Row Group stores a subset of the dataset.

We intentionally won't dive deeper into Row Groups yet—they deserve an entire chapter of their own.

For now, simply remember that the data section consists of one or more Row Groups.

docs.title: File Metadata (Footer)
docs.text:
The footer is the most important part of a Parquet file.

It describes everything needed to read the data.

Typical metadata includes:

  • Schema
  • Number of Row Groups
  • Compression codec
  • Encoding used
  • Statistics
  • Location (offset) of every Row Group
  • Number of rows

Notice the scope of this metadata.

It describes one Parquet file, not an entire table.

This distinction becomes important later when we study Hive and Apache Iceberg.

docs.title: Footer Length
docs.text:
Immediately before the closing magic bytes, Parquet stores the size of the footer.

+----------------------+
| Footer Metadata      |
+----------------------+
| Footer Length = 2048 |
+----------------------+
| PAR1                 |
+----------------------+

This small integer tells the reader exactly how many bytes to move backwards in order to locate the footer.

Without it, the reader would have to scan the entire file looking for metadata.

docs.title: Why Is the Footer at the End?
docs.text:
This is one of Parquet's most elegant design decisions.

Imagine writing a new Parquet file.

Initially, the writer doesn't know:

  • How many Row Groups will be created.
  • How large each Row Group will be.
  • What statistics each Row Group will contain.
  • Where each Row Group will be located within the file.

All of this information becomes available only after the data has been written.

Therefore, Parquet follows this sequence:

  1. Write the data.
  2. Collect metadata while writing.
  3. Write the footer.
  4. Record the footer length.
  5. Write the closing magic bytes.

This allows the metadata to accurately describe the completed file.

docs.title: How Spark Reads a Parquet File
docs.text:
When Spark opens a Parquet file, it does not start by reading the data.

Instead, it works backwards.

Read last 4 bytes
        ↓
Verify "PAR1"
        ↓
Read footer length
        ↓
Jump directly to footer
        ↓
Read metadata
        ↓
Decide which Row Groups to read

This is why Spark can make intelligent decisions before scanning the data itself.

For example, Spark can determine:

  • the schema,
  • the number of Row Groups,
  • available statistics,
  • and the compression algorithm

without reading the entire file.

docs.title: What We Learned
docs.text:
A Parquet file is more than a compressed binary blob.

It has a carefully designed layout consisting of:

  • A data section containing one or more Row Groups.
  • A footer describing how to interpret that data.
  • Magic bytes and a footer length that allow readers to quickly locate the metadata.

This layout enables engines like Spark to inspect metadata first and read only the data required by a query.

docs.title: What's Next?
docs.text:
Now that we understand the overall layout of a Parquet file, we are ready to study one of its most important building blocks:

Row Groups

We'll answer questions such as:

  • What exactly is a Row Group?
  • Why do Row Groups exist?
  • Why are they the unit of parallelism?
  • How do they enable efficient analytical queries?

docs.title: Row Groups — The Unit of Parallelism in a Parquet File
Why This Chapter?
docs.text:
In the previous chapter, we learned that a Parquet file consists of two major sections:

  • Data (one or more Row Groups)
  • Footer (metadata)

This naturally raises the next question:

Why does Parquet divide data into Row Groups instead of storing one giant block of columnar data?

Understanding Row Groups is one of the most important steps toward understanding how Spark efficiently processes Parquet files and, later, why Apache Iceberg builds upon Parquet rather than replacing it.

docs.title: Imagine a Parquet File Without Row Groups
docs.text:
Suppose we have a Parquet file containing one billion rows.

Without Row Groups, the file would conceptually look like this:

+---------------------------------------------+
|                                             |
|           One Huge Column Store             |
|                                             |
+---------------------------------------------+

Although the data is stored column by column, it still behaves like one enormous unit.

Now imagine Spark needs to execute:

SELECT *
FROM events
WHERE event_date = '2026-06-01'

Several problems immediately appear:

  • Can multiple executors independently process different regions of the file?
  • Can Spark skip only part of the file?
  • Can metadata describe different portions of the data separately?

The answer is essentially no.

The file is simply too coarse-grained.

docs.title: Enter Row Groups
docs.text:
Parquet solves this by dividing the data into Row Groups.

Conceptually, the file now looks like:

+---------------------------------------------+
| Row Group 1                                 |
+---------------------------------------------+
| Row Group 2                                 |
+---------------------------------------------+
| Row Group 3                                 |
+---------------------------------------------+
| Row Group 4                                 |
+---------------------------------------------+
| Footer                                      |
+---------------------------------------------+

Each Row Group contains a subset of the rows.

For example:

Row Group Rows RG1 1 – 1,000,000 RG2 1,000,001 – 2,000,000 RG3 2,000,001 – 3,000,000 RG4 3,000,001 – 4,000,000

Notice something important.

The rows remain in their original order.

Parquet is not partitioning or shuffling the data.

It is simply breaking the file into independently readable regions.

docs.title: Why Are Row Groups So Important?
docs.text:
A Row Group is much more than a chunk of rows.

It is the smallest independently readable unit within a Parquet file.

Each Row Group has its own:

  • Column data
  • Compression
  • Encodings
  • Statistics (minimum, maximum, null count)
  • Metadata

This means every Row Group can be processed independently.

docs.title: Row Groups Enable Parallel Processing
docs.text:
