docs.title: Concept
docs.text:
Apache Spark transformations can broadly be categorized into:

  1. Narrow transformations
  2. Wide transformations

The key difference lies in whether data movement (shuffle) is required across partitions.

This distinction is extremely important because shuffle is one of the most expensive operations in distributed systems.

docs.title: Why This Concept Exists
docs.text:
Spark processes data in distributed partitions.

Some operations can be performed independently within each partition, while others require records from multiple partitions to be grouped together.

This distinction impacts: - Performance - Network utilization - Memory usage - Number of stages in execution - Scalability

Understanding narrow vs wide transformations helps reason about: - Why some jobs are fast - Why some jobs create additional stages - Why some jobs trigger shuffle - Why some jobs become expensive at scale

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A narrow transformation is a transformation where each output partition depends on data from only a single input partition.

No data movement across partitions is required.

docs.title: Internal Mental Model
docs.text:
Imagine Spark already divided the dataset into partitions:

Partition 1
Partition 2
Partition 3

If a transformation can be executed independently within each partition, then it is narrow.

Examples: - filter - select - withColumn - map

Each worker processes only its local partition.

No communication between workers is required.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
filtered_df = df.filter("event_type = 'purchase'")

Spark simply scans each partition locally and filters matching rows.

No shuffle occurs.

docs.title: Spark Execution Behavior
docs.text: Typical execution characteristics: - Usually remains within the same stage - No shuffle boundary - No network data movement - Faster execution - Better scalability

docs.title: Common Narrow Transformations
docs.text: Transformation Reason filter Operates locally on partition select Column projection only withColumn Row-wise computation map Local row transformation flatMap Local expansion union Appends partitions

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A wide transformation is a transformation where output partitions depend on data from multiple input partitions.

Spark must redistribute data across the cluster.

This redistribution is called shuffle.

docs.title: Internal Mental Model
docs.text:
Suppose data is partitioned like this:

Partition event_type P1 view P2 purchase P3 view

Now consider:

df.groupBy("event_type").count()

To compute final counts: - all view records must come together - all purchase records must come together

Spark cannot complete aggregation independently within each partition.

Hence Spark performs: 1. Partial aggregation locally 2. Shuffle data across partitions 3. Final aggregation after redistribution

docs.title: Multi-Phase Aggregation
docs.text: Wide transformations often execute in multiple phases.

docs.title: Stage 1 — Partial Aggregation
docs.text:
Each partition computes local aggregates.

Example:

Partition Local Aggregate P1 {view: 100} P2 {purchase: 20} P3 {view: 80}

This reduces shuffle size.

docs.title: Shuffle Boundary
docs.text:
Spark redistributes data using partitioning logic similar to:

hash(key) % number_of_shuffle_partitions

This guarantees: - all matching keys go to the same reducer partition

Important: A reducer partition may contain multiple keys.

docs.title: Stage 2 — Final Aggregation
docs.text:
Spark merges partial aggregates:

view → 100 + 80 = 180

Final output is generated.

docs.title: Spark Execution Behavior
docs.text: Wide transformations usually: - Create additional stages - Introduce shuffle boundaries - Require network communication - Increase disk and memory usage - Are more expensive than narrow transformations

docs.title: Common Wide Transformations
docs.text: Transformation Why Shuffle Is Needed groupBy Same keys must come together join Matching keys must align distinct Duplicate detection across partitions repartition Explicit redistribution orderBy Global ordering dropDuplicates Requires global comparison

docs.title: Spark UI Observation
docs.text:
Wide transformations become very visible in Spark UI.

Typical observations: - Additional stages - Shuffle Read - Shuffle Write - Exchange operators in physical plan

docs.title: Physical Plan Example
docs.text:
For:

df.groupBy("event_type").count()

Spark may generate a plan resembling:

HashAggregate
  Exchange
    HashAggregate

Meaning: 1. Partial aggregation 2. Shuffle (Exchange) 3. Final aggregation

This is one of Spark's most fundamental execution patterns.

docs.title: Narrow Transformations
docs.text:
• Faster
  • Partition-local
  • Minimal network usage
  • Better throughput

docs.title: Wide Transformations
docs.text:
• More expensive
  • Network heavy
  • May spill to disk
  • Can create skew problems
  • Require careful partition tuning

docs.title: Misconception 1
docs.text:
Wide transformations always create one partition per key.

Reality: - Spark hashes keys across reducer partitions - Multiple keys may exist within same partition

docs.title: Misconception 2
docs.text:
Shuffle means moving entire raw dataset.

Reality: Spark often performs partial aggregation before shuffle to reduce data movement.

docs.title: Misconception 3
docs.text:
limit() is a wide transformation.

Reality: limit() itself is not inherently wide, though Spark may still scan multiple partitions to satisfy correctness guarantees.

docs.title: Operational Impact
docs.text:
Understanding narrow vs wide transformations is critical for: - Query optimization - Shuffle tuning - Partition sizing - Debugging slow jobs - Avoiding skew - Designing scalable pipelines

Most Spark performance issues are ultimately related to: - Excessive shuffle - Poor partitioning - Wide transformation amplification

docs.title: Partition Size != Actual Runtime Memory Usage
Concept
docs.text:
Initially, it may seem intuitive that if a Spark execution partition is roughly 128MB and the executor has 2GB RAM, then processing should always succeed comfortably.

However, this assumption is incorrect because: - partition size represents input data size on disk - runtime memory usage represents fully materialized in-memory execution state

These two numbers can differ significantly.

docs.title: Why This Happens
docs.text:
Spark does not process raw bytes directly from disk.

During execution: - CSV/text data gets parsed - rows become JVM objects - strings get allocated - execution metadata gets created - serialization/deserialization buffers are allocated - shuffle and aggregation buffers may appear

As a result: - in-memory representation often becomes much larger than on-disk size

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Suppose a CSV partition is:

128MB on disk

During processing, Spark may allocate memory for: - parsed rows - Java/Python objects - UTF string representations - InternalRow structures - task execution buffers - S3/network buffers - JVM overhead

Actual memory consumption may therefore become: - several hundred MB - or even multiple GB in extreme cases

depending on workload complexity.

docs.title: CSV Is Especially Expensive
docs.text:
CSV is: - row-oriented - text-based - schema-less at storage level

Spark must: - parse text - infer/cast types - allocate strings - deserialize rows

This creates substantial CPU and memory overhead.

This is one major reason modern analytical systems prefer: - Parquet - ORC - Iceberg-backed tables - Delta Lake

which use: - binary formats - columnar storage - typed encoding

docs.title: Spark Memory Is Shared Across Multiple Concerns
docs.text:
Executor memory is not used only for partition data.

It is also consumed by: - JVM heap - execution memory - shuffle buffers - aggregation state - serialization/deserialization - task metadata - Python worker processes - network buffers - filesystem connector buffers

This means even relatively small partitions can trigger memory pressure.

docs.title: Parallelism Multiplies Memory Usage
docs.text:
If an executor runs multiple tasks concurrently:

2 cores → 2 simultaneous tasks

then memory usage increases accordingly.

Example:

128MB partition × 2 concurrent tasks

does NOT imply only:

256MB memory usage

because runtime overhead also multiplies.

docs.title: Schema Inference Is Expensive
docs.text:
CSV schema inference may: - scan data multiple times - sample rows aggressively - allocate parsing structures

This increases: - IO - CPU - memory pressure

In production systems, explicit schemas are generally preferred.

docs.title: PySpark Adds Additional Overhead
docs.text:
PySpark execution involves: - JVM executors - Python worker processes

Data often crosses:

JVM ↔ Python boundary

through serialization/deserialization.

This introduces: - additional memory overhead - extra CPU cost - buffer allocations

docs.title: Operational Impact
docs.text:
Spark memory tuning is influenced by: - file format - partition sizing - task concurrency - shuffle behavior - serialization overhead - execution engine internals

This means: - executor sizing is a workload-specific tuning exercise - raw file size alone is not enough to estimate memory requirements

docs.title: Most Important Learning
docs.text:
Execution partition size should NOT be interpreted as:

actual runtime memory usage

Distributed compute systems operate on: - parsed - deserialized - materialized - transformed

data structures whose runtime footprint may greatly exceed original storage size.

docs.title: repartition() vs coalesce() in Apache Spark
Concept
docs.text:
repartition() and coalesce() are Spark operations used to change the number of downstream execution partitions.

Although both modify partition counts, they behave very differently internally.

Understanding this distinction is critical for: - shuffle optimization - partition tuning - output file sizing - reducing unnecessary data movement - improving distributed execution efficiency

docs.title: First Principles
docs.text:
Partitions are the unit of: - distributed execution - task scheduling - parallelism

Changing partition count changes: - number of downstream tasks - execution topology - workload distribution

However:

changing partition count
does NOT always mean
physically redistributing all rows

This distinction is the key difference between: - repartition() - coalesce()

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
repartition() performs:

full global redistribution of rows

Spark: 1. destroys old partition layout 2. shuffles rows globally 3. creates entirely new partitions

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
df.repartition(10)

Spark: - redistributes rows across executors - creates 10 new balanced partitions - performs full shuffle exchange

docs.title: Important Internal Behavior
docs.text:
repartition() always triggers:

full shuffle exchange

This includes: - shuffle write - shuffle read - reducer fetch - network redistribution

Rows may move: - from any partition - to any new partition

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of:

df.repartition(10)

as:

"destroy old partitioning,
rebalance dataset globally"

Spark rebuilds the partition layout entirely.

docs.title: How repartition() Works Internally
docs.text:
Suppose:

200 upstream partitions

Now:

df.repartition(2)

Spark: 1. hashes rows into new reducer partitions 2. writes shuffle files locally 3. reducers fetch shuffle blocks 4. creates 2 entirely new partitions

This is classic shuffle behavior.

docs.title: Important Property
docs.text:
After repartition: - old partition layout no longer matters - new global partitioning created - workload balancing improves

This is why repartition: - is expensive - but often produces better balance

docs.title: Rebalancing Skewed Data
docs.text:
df.repartition(200)

Improves: - workload distribution - cluster utilization

docs.title: Before Joins/Aggregations
docs.text: Balanced partitions improve: - shuffle performance - parallelism

docs.title: Partitioning By Key
docs.text:
df.repartition(50, "user_id")

Rows with same key tend to land together.

Useful for: - joins - aggregations

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
coalesce() primarily changes:

how downstream tasks consume partitions

without rebuilding the global partition layout.

This is the most important mental model.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
df.coalesce(2)

Spark tries: - reducing downstream task count - collapsing partition consumption - avoiding full shuffle exchange

docs.title: Important Internal Behavior
docs.text:
By default:

df.coalesce(2)

uses:

shuffle=False

Meaning: - no full shuffle exchange - no global redistribution - no reducer fetch protocol

This is fundamentally different from repartition.

docs.title: The Most Important Insight
docs.text:
coalesce() usually does NOT: - physically reorganize rows - globally redistribute data - create entirely new partition layouts

Instead:

fewer downstream tasks
consume multiple upstream partitions

This is the core behavior.

docs.title: Internal Mental Model
docs.text:
Suppose:

200 upstream partitions

Now:

df.coalesce(2)

Spark may logically schedule:

Downstream Task Reads Task A partitions 0-99 Task B partitions 100-199

Notice: - upstream partition files remain unchanged - no full shuffle exchange occurs - no global row redistribution happens

Spark mostly changes: - downstream execution topology

This is why coalesce is much cheaper.

docs.title: Extremely Important Clarification
docs.text:
When people say:

coalesce avoids shuffle

they usually mean:

coalesce avoids FULL shuffle exchange

This does NOT necessarily mean: - absolutely zero coordination - zero remote reads - zero data movement

But Spark avoids: - expensive all-to-all redistribution

That is the key distinction.

docs.title: repartition() vs coalesce()
docs.text: Feature repartition() coalesce() Full shuffle exchange Yes Usually No Global redistribution Yes No New partition layout Yes No Reducer fetch protocol Yes Usually No Task count reduction Yes Yes Increase partitions Yes Not meaningful Decrease partitions Yes Yes Balancing quality Better Potentially skewed Cost High Lower

docs.title: Why coalesce() Is Cheaper
docs.text:
Because Spark avoids: - shuffle write - shuffle read - reducer fetch - global row redistribution - expensive network exchange

Instead: - fewer downstream tasks consume existing partitions

This drastically reduces: - network IO - disk IO - shuffle overhead

docs.title: Important Limitation
docs.text:
Because coalesce preserves original layout:

existing skew may remain

Example:

Partition Size P1 5 GB P2 50 MB

Coalesce may still produce: - imbalanced downstream tasks

Because rows are NOT globally redistributed.

docs.title: coalesce(shuffle=True)
docs.text:
Spark also supports:

df.coalesce(2, shuffle=True)

This performs: - actual shuffle exchange - redistribution behavior closer to repartition

Most engineers rarely use this explicitly.

docs.title: repartition()
docs.text:
Suitable for: - increasing partitions - decreasing partitions - rebalancing workloads

Because Spark rebuilds partition layout globally.

docs.title: coalesce()
docs.text:
Primarily intended for:

reducing downstream task count cheaply

without expensive redistribution.

Not intended for: - meaningful repartition balancing

docs.title: repartition()
docs.text: Used when: - improving balance - increasing parallelism - optimizing joins - handling skew - redistributing workloads

docs.title: coalesce()
docs.text: Used when: - reducing output file count - optimizing final writes - reducing small files - collapsing excessive partitions

docs.title: Common Example
docs.text:
df.coalesce(1).write.parquet(...)

Goal: - produce fewer output files

Spark tries: - reducing downstream write tasks without: - globally reshuffling rows

docs.title: Important Caveat
docs.text:
coalesce(1) may: - destroy parallelism - bottleneck execution - overload single task/executor

Dangerous for: - very large datasets

Usually acceptable only for: - small outputs - debugging - demos

docs.title: repartition()
docs.text: Usually shows: - shuffle stages - Exchange operators - shuffle read/write metrics

docs.title: coalesce()
docs.text: Usually shows: - fewer shuffle operations - simpler execution plans - reduced downstream task count

docs.title: Misconception 1
docs.text:
Changing partition count always means global redistribution.

Reality: coalesce() often only changes downstream partition consumption.

docs.title: Misconception 2
docs.text:
coalesce() physically merges rows into new partitions.

Reality: Spark often preserves existing partition layout and changes downstream task topology.

docs.title: Misconception 3
docs.text:
coalesce() means zero data movement.

Reality: Some coordination or remote reads may still occur.

Spark simply avoids: - full shuffle exchange protocol

docs.title: Misconception 4
docs.text:
repartition() is always bad.

Reality: Sometimes repartition dramatically improves: - balancing - parallelism - overall runtime

docs.title: repartition()
docs.text:
Destroy old partitioning,
redistribute rows globally,
create entirely new partition layout

docs.title: coalesce()
docs.text:
Keep existing partition layout mostly intact,
reduce downstream task count,
allow fewer tasks to consume multiple upstream partitions

This distinction is foundational for Spark optimization and distributed systems reasoning.

docs.title: Concept
docs.text:
Shuffle is one of the most important concepts in Apache Spark.

Shuffle occurs when Spark needs to redistribute data across partitions/executors so that related records end up together.

This usually happens during: - groupBy - joins - orderBy - distinct - repartition

Shuffle is fundamentally: - distributed data movement - distributed coordination - distributed aggregation

It is often the most expensive operation in Spark workloads.

docs.title: Why Shuffle Exists
docs.text:
Spark initially processes data partition-locally.

Example:

Partition Records P1 view P2 purchase P3 view

Now suppose we execute:

df.groupBy("event_type").count()

To compute final counts: - all "view" rows must end up together - all "purchase" rows must end up together

But these rows currently exist across multiple partitions.

Spark therefore needs to: 1. redistribute records 2. regroup data by key 3. aggregate related records together

This redistribution process is called shuffle.

docs.title: Extremely Important Mental Model
docs.text:
Without shuffle:

partitions are independently processable

Spark behaves almost embarrassingly parallel.

Each partition: - executes independently - requires little coordination

With shuffle:

Spark becomes distributed coordination system

Executors now: - exchange data - coordinate processing - synchronize stage execution - perform distributed aggregation

This is why shuffle is expensive.

docs.title: Shuffle Lifecycle
docs.text:
Shuffle is not a single operation.

It is a multi-stage distributed protocol.

docs.title: Stage 1 — Map Side Processing
docs.text:
Suppose we execute:

df.groupBy("event_type").count()

Input partitions are processed by map tasks.

Each map task: 1. reads its partition 2. performs partial aggregation 3. hashes records into reducer buckets 4. writes shuffle outputs locally

docs.title: Map-Side Aggregation
docs.text:
Spark tries to reduce shuffle volume early.

Example:

Partition Partial Aggregation P1 {view:100} P2 {purchase:20} P3 {view:80}

Instead of shuffling every individual row: - Spark may shuffle partial aggregates

This optimization is called:

map-side aggregation

This significantly reduces network traffic.

docs.title: Important Clarification
docs.text:
Not all shuffle operations involve aggregation.

Example:

df.repartition(10)

Triggers shuffle: - but no aggregation occurs

So:

shuffle != aggregation

Aggregation is sometimes an optimization applied before shuffle.

docs.title: Stage 2 — Shuffle Write
docs.text:
After processing: - map tasks hash records by reducer partition

Conceptually:

hash(key) % num_shuffle_partitions

determines: - which reducer partition receives the record

Each executor then writes shuffle blocks locally.

Example:

Executor A
  shuffle block for reducer 0
  shuffle block for reducer 1
  shuffle block for reducer 2

This is an extremely important detail.

Spark does NOT immediately stream rows directly between executors.

Instead:

shuffle output is first materialized locally

usually: - on local disk - sometimes memory + spill

docs.title: Stage 3 — Shuffle Read
docs.text:
Reducer tasks start later.

Each reducer knows:

"I need shuffle partition X"

Reducers then: 1. contact all executors 2. fetch required shuffle blocks 3. merge received data 4. perform final aggregation

This is fundamentally:

pull-based shuffle

Reducers pull shuffle blocks from executors.

This is a very important mental model.

docs.title: Why Spark Uses Pull-Based Shuffle
docs.text:
Map tasks and reduce tasks are decoupled through shuffle materialization.

This enables: - independent task retries - fault tolerance - flexible scheduling - asynchronous execution

Reducers may: - start later - retry independently - execute on different executors

Materialized shuffle outputs make this possible.

docs.title: Shuffle Creates Stage Boundaries
docs.text:
This is one of Spark's most important execution rules.

Reducers cannot begin until: - map-side shuffle outputs are fully available

Therefore:

shuffle creates synchronization barriers

This is why: - wide transformations create new stages

Example:

df.groupBy(...).count()

typically produces: - one stage for map-side processing - another stage for reduce-side aggregation

docs.title: Shuffle Is Expensive
docs.text: Shuffle is expensive because it introduces:

docs.title: 1. Network IO
docs.text:
Executors exchange shuffle blocks over the network.

Distributed network communication is expensive.

docs.title: 2. Disk IO
docs.text:
Shuffle outputs are often written to local disk.

Large shuffles may generate: - huge intermediate files - heavy disk activity

docs.title: 3. Serialization & Deserialization
docs.text:
Data transferred between executors must be: - serialized - transmitted - deserialized

This introduces CPU overhead.

docs.title: 4. Sorting & Merging
docs.text:
Shuffle often requires: - sorting - merging streams - grouping keys

These operations consume: - CPU - memory - disk

docs.title: 5. Synchronization Delays
docs.text:
Reducers often wait for: - all map tasks to finish

This creates execution barriers.

docs.title: Exchange Operator
docs.text:
In physical plans:

Exchange

usually indicates: - shuffle boundary

This is one of the most important operators to recognize in Spark physical plans.

docs.title: Shuffle Partitions
docs.text:
Shuffle outputs are redistributed into:

spark.sql.shuffle.partitions

Default value:

200

This setting determines: - number of reducer partitions

docs.title: Partition Tradeoffs
docs.text:
Too many shuffle partitions: - scheduling overhead increases - tiny tasks created

Too few shuffle partitions: - tasks become huge - memory pressure increases - skew worsens

Proper partition sizing is extremely important.

docs.title: Shuffle and repartition()
docs.text:
df.repartition(10)

Always triggers shuffle because: - Spark performs full redistribution - rows may move anywhere

This creates balanced partitions but is expensive.

docs.title: Shuffle and coalesce()
docs.text:
df.coalesce(2)

Usually avoids full shuffle.

Instead of: - globally redistributing rows

Spark tries: - collapsing existing partitions together

This minimizes: - network movement - shuffle overhead

docs.title: Data Skew
docs.text:
One of the biggest real-world Spark problems is:

data skew

Example:

event_type Frequency view 99% purchase 1%

Now: - one reducer partition becomes enormous - others remain tiny

Symptoms: - one slow task - long-tail execution - executor memory pressure - spill to disk

Skew is one of the most important production optimization problems.

docs.title: Spill To Disk
docs.text:
If shuffle memory becomes insufficient:

Spark spills intermediate data: - to local disk

This prevents: - executor OOM crashes

But increases: - latency - disk IO

docs.title: Spark UI Observation
docs.text:
Shuffle becomes visible in Spark UI through: - additional stages - shuffle read metrics - shuffle write metrics - Exchange operators - long-running reducers

The Spark UI is one of the best tools for understanding shuffle behavior.

docs.title: Misconception 1
docs.text:
Shuffle means direct row streaming between executors.

Reality:

map tasks first materialize shuffle outputs locally,
reducers later fetch shuffle blocks

Spark fundamentally uses pull-based shuffle.

docs.title: Misconception 2
docs.text:
Shuffle is purely memory operation.

Reality: Shuffle heavily involves: - disk - network - serialization - sorting

docs.title: Misconception 3
docs.text:
Only joins trigger shuffle.

Reality: Many wide transformations trigger shuffle: - groupBy - orderBy - distinct - repartition

docs.title: Misconception 4
docs.text:
More partitions always improve performance.

Reality: Too many partitions create scheduling overhead.

docs.title: Operational Impact
docs.text:
Most Spark performance bottlenecks are related to: - shuffle volume - skew - partition imbalance - network saturation - spill to disk

Understanding shuffle is critical for: - Spark optimization - distributed systems reasoning - debugging production pipelines

docs.title: Most Important Mental Shift
docs.text:
Distributed system cost is often dominated by:

data movement

rather than: - actual computation

In distributed systems:

moving data is often more expensive than processing data

This is one of the deepest lessons in Spark and distributed computing.

docs.title: Concept
docs.text:
Apache Spark operations are broadly categorized into:

  1. Transformations
  2. Actions

Understanding this distinction is fundamental because Spark uses lazy evaluation.

Transformations build execution plans, while actions trigger actual execution.

docs.title: Why This Concept Exists
docs.text:
Spark is designed as a distributed computation engine.

Instead of executing each operation immediately, Spark first builds an optimized execution plan (DAG).

This enables Spark to: - Optimize execution - Reduce unnecessary computation - Combine operations efficiently - Minimize data movement - Generate efficient physical plans

Without lazy evaluation, distributed processing would become significantly less efficient.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Transformations are operations that define how data should be modified or processed.

Transformations do NOT execute immediately.

Instead, they create a new DataFrame or RDD representing a new logical execution plan.

docs.title: Internal Mental Model
docs.text:
Suppose we write:

filtered = df.filter("event_type = 'purchase'")

selected = filtered.select("user_id", "product_id")

Spark does NOT: - read the dataset immediately - filter rows immediately - select columns immediately

Instead Spark internally builds a logical DAG similar to:

Read CSV
    ↓
Filter purchase events
    ↓
Select required columns

This execution plan is called lineage.

No actual computation happens yet.

docs.title: Characteristics of Transformations
docs.text: Transformations: - Are lazily evaluated - Build lineage/DAG - Return new DataFrames or RDDs - Do not materialize results immediately

docs.title: Common Transformations
docs.text: Transformation Description filter Filters rows select Selects columns withColumn Adds/modifies columns map Row-level transformation flatMap Expands rows groupBy Groups records orderBy Sorts records repartition Redistributes partitions coalesce Reduces partitions join Combines datasets

docs.title: Narrow vs Wide Transformations
docs.text:
Transformations can further be categorized into:

Type Requires Shuffle? Narrow Transformation No Wide Transformation Yes

Examples: - filter() → narrow transformation - groupBy() → wide transformation

Wide transformations introduce shuffle and stage boundaries.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Actions trigger actual execution of the DAG.

When an action is called: - Spark optimizes the plan - Jobs are created - Stages are generated - Tasks are scheduled - Executors begin computation

This is the moment when lazy evaluation ends.

docs.title: Internal Mental Model
docs.text:
Suppose we now execute:

selected.count()

Spark now: 1. Builds optimized physical plan 2. Creates jobs and stages 3. Launches tasks 4. Reads data 5. Executes transformations 6. Produces final result

Actual computation finally begins.

docs.title: Characteristics of Actions
docs.text: Actions: - Trigger DAG execution - Materialize results - Return concrete output - Start distributed computation

docs.title: Common Actions
docs.text: Action Description count Counts records show Displays rows collect Brings data to driver write Persists output take Returns first N rows first Returns first row foreach Executes side effects save Writes output

docs.title: Transformations Return Logical Plans
docs.text:
Example:

filtered = df.filter(...)

Returns: - another DataFrame - another logical execution plan

No computation yet.

docs.title: Actions Return Materialized Results
docs.text:
Example:

df.count()

Returns: - concrete integer value

Example:

df.write.parquet(...)

Produces: - actual files on storage

docs.title: Lazy Evaluation
docs.text:
Spark uses lazy evaluation to: - Combine multiple transformations - Optimize query plans - Avoid unnecessary computation - Minimize shuffle - Reduce disk and network usage

This is one of Spark's core architectural principles.

docs.title: Example Workflow
docs.text:
df = spark.read.csv("events.csv")

filtered = df.filter("event_type = 'purchase'")

selected = filtered.select("user_id")

selected.count()

Execution behavior:

Step Execution? read No filter No select No count Yes

Only the action triggers execution.

docs.title: Catalyst Optimizer
docs.text:
Before execution, Spark uses Catalyst Optimizer to: - Combine transformations - Push filters down - Remove unnecessary columns - Reorder operations - Generate optimized physical plans

This optimization happens before actions execute.

docs.title: Spark UI Observation
docs.text:
Transformations alone usually do not appear in Spark UI because no execution occurs.

Once an action is called: - Jobs appear - Stages appear - Tasks get scheduled - Shuffle becomes visible

docs.title: Misconception 1
docs.text:
Transformations immediately execute.

Reality: Transformations only build lineage.

docs.title: Misconception 2
docs.text:
Each transformation creates a separate job.

Reality: Spark combines transformations into optimized execution plans.

docs.title: Misconception 3
docs.text:
Transformations are always cheap.

Reality: Wide transformations may trigger expensive shuffle operations.

docs.title: Misconception 4
docs.text:
Actions are always safe.

Reality: Some actions like collect() may overload driver memory by bringing large datasets to the driver.

docs.title: Operational Impact
docs.text:
Understanding transformations vs actions is critical for: - Debugging Spark jobs - Avoiding accidental recomputation - Optimizing performance - Understanding Spark UI - Designing scalable pipelines - Efficient caching strategies

This concept forms the foundation for: - Lazy evaluation - DAG execution - Query optimization - Caching and persistence

docs.title: Users Dataset
docs.text:
user_id country 1 IN 2 US

In a distributed cluster:

  • rows from both datasets may exist on different executors
  • Spark cannot directly join them

Before joining:

  • matching keys must be colocated together

This is the core distributed join problem.

docs.title: Two Fundamental Distributed Join Strategies
docs.text:
Distributed systems generally solve joins using one of two approaches:

Strategy Idea Shuffle Join Move matching keys together Broadcast Join Replicate small dataset everywhere

SortMergeJoin is Spark's default shuffle-based join strategy for large datasets.

docs.title: Example Pipeline
docs.text:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

events_df = spark.read.csv(
    "s3a://clickstream/2019-Nov.csv",
    header=True
)

users_df = spark.read.parquet(
    "s3a://users/users.parquet"
)

joined_df = events_df.join(
    users_df,
    "user_id"
)

joined_df.count()

docs.title: Initial Plan vs Final Plan
docs.text:
Spark physical plans exist in two forms:

Plan Type Meaning Initial Plan Optimizer's intended execution strategy Final Plan Runtime AQE-optimized execution strategy

Before execution:

  • Spark only knows estimated statistics

During execution:

  • AQE collects actual runtime statistics
  • Spark may optimize partitioning and execution strategies dynamically

This is why Spark shows:

AdaptiveSparkPlan

and:

isFinalPlan=true

after execution completes.

docs.title: 1. Scan Source Data
docs.text: Spark first scans both datasets.

docs.title: Events Dataset
docs.text: Scan csv

docs.title: Users Dataset
docs.text: Scan parquet

docs.title: Important Observation: CSV vs Parquet
docs.text:
CSV scan:

Batched: false

Parquet scan:

Batched: true

Why?

Parquet supports:

  • vectorized columnar reads

CSV does not.

This is one major reason why Parquet significantly outperforms CSV.

docs.title: 2. Catalyst Adds Null Filters
docs.text:
Spark automatically inserts:

Filter isnotnull(user_id)

on both sides.

Why?

Because:

  • null values cannot efficiently participate in equality joins

This optimization is automatically added by Catalyst.

docs.title: 3. Exchange — Shuffle Boundary
docs.text:
Spark then performs:

Exchange
Arguments: hashpartitioning(user_id, 200)

This is the most important distributed phase.

Spark repartitions BOTH datasets using:

hash(user_id) % 200

This guarantees:

same user_ids land in same partition

This is the core requirement for distributed joins.

docs.title: Extremely Important Clarification
docs.text:
Exchange is a logical shuffle boundary.

It does NOT literally mean:

  • Spark immediately pushes rows over network

Instead it means:

data must be redistributed by key

docs.title: Actual Shuffle Mechanics
docs.text: Shuffle internally happens in two phases.

docs.title: Map-Side Shuffle Phase
docs.text:
Map-side tasks:

  1. read rows
  2. hash rows by partition key
  3. write shuffle files LOCALLY

Example:

Executor A:
  partition-0.data
  partition-1.data
  partition-2.data

At this point:

  • reducers have NOT fetched anything yet

docs.title: Reduce-Side Shuffle Phase
docs.text:
Reducer tasks later:

  1. contact all executors
  2. fetch required shuffle partitions
  3. merge fetched data locally

This means Spark shuffle is fundamentally:

pull-based

NOT:

  • push-based

This design comes from Hadoop MapReduce architecture.

docs.title: Important Mental Model
docs.text:
Exchange
=
logical repartitioning boundary

Internally implemented via:
  map-side shuffle writes
  +
  reducer-side shuffle fetches

This is one of the most important Spark internals concepts.

docs.title: 4. ShuffleQueryStage
docs.text:
After shuffle writes complete, Spark creates:

ShuffleQueryStage

This represents:

  • materialized shuffle output
  • a stable shuffle boundary
  • runtime statistics collection point

Example:

Statistics(sizeInBytes=2.0 GiB, rowCount=6.75E+7)

Spark now knows:

  • actual shuffle size
  • actual row counts

This information is used by AQE.

docs.title: 5. AQEShuffleRead
docs.text:
Spark then performs:

AQEShuffleRead
Arguments: coalesced

This means:

  • AQE dynamically reduced shuffle partition count

Instead of:

  • reading all original shuffle partitions

Spark may:

  • merge tiny partitions together

This improves:

  • scheduling overhead
  • tiny task inefficiency
  • resource utilization

docs.title: 6. Sort Within Partition
docs.text:
After reducers fetch shuffle data:

Spark performs:

Sort

Important:

Sorting happens:

within EACH partition

NOT:

  • globally across cluster

This distinction is extremely important.

docs.title: Why Sorting Is Required
docs.text:
Once both datasets are:

  • partitioned identically
  • sorted by join key

Spark can perform:

sequential merge join

similar to:

  • merge step in merge sort

This approach is:

  • memory efficient
  • scalable
  • streaming-friendly

docs.title: 7. SortMergeJoin Execution
docs.text:
Now both sides contain:

  • matching partition topology
  • sorted rows

Spark can perform local merge join execution.

Important:

network movement already completed earlier

during:

  • Exchange / shuffle phase

The actual SortMergeJoin operator is:

  • local CPU computation
  • not network transfer

docs.title: Extremely Important Distinction
docs.text:
Phase Purpose Exchange Distributed data movement AQEShuffleRead Reducer-side shuffle fetch Sort Local ordering SortMergeJoin Local merge computation

This is a foundational Spark execution concept.

docs.title: 8. ColumnarToRow
docs.text:
Parquet scan shows:

ColumnarToRow

Why?

Parquet internally uses:

  • columnar vectorized representation

But:

  • SortMergeJoin operates on row-based execution

Spark therefore converts:

  • columnar batches → rows

This becomes important later while learning:

  • Tungsten
  • vectorized execution
  • whole-stage codegen

docs.title: 9. Count Aggregation
docs.text:
The query ends with:

joined_df.count()

Spark implements this using distributed aggregation.

docs.title: Partial Aggregation
docs.text:
Each partition first computes:

partial_count

locally.

This reduces:

  • network traffic
  • shuffle volume

docs.title: Final Aggregation
docs.text:
Spark then performs:

Exchange
Arguments: SinglePartition

This gathers:

  • all partial counts
  • into a single reducer partition

Then Spark computes:

final count

This is a classic distributed aggregation pattern.

docs.title: Why SortMergeJoin Scales Well
docs.text:
Unlike large hash joins:

  • SortMergeJoin does not require huge in-memory hash tables

Instead Spark:

  • streams through sorted datasets sequentially

This makes it:

  • more memory efficient
  • better for very large datasets

docs.title: Why SortMergeJoin Is Expensive
docs.text:
Even though merge computation itself is efficient:

shuffle is extremely expensive because Spark must:

  • serialize rows
  • partition rows
  • spill to disk
  • transfer data across network
  • fetch remote shuffle blocks
  • merge shuffle files
  • sort reducer partitions

Most join cost usually comes from:

shuffle

NOT:

  • merge computation itself

docs.title: 1. Distributed Joins Mean Colocating Keys
docs.text:
matching keys must land together

This is the core distributed join requirement.

docs.title: 2. Exchange Is Logical
docs.text:
Exchange represents:

  • repartitioning intent

Internally implemented via:

  • map-side shuffle writes
  • reducer-side shuffle fetches

docs.title: 3. Shuffle Is Pull-Based
docs.text:
Reducers:

  • fetch shuffle blocks from executors

Spark shuffle is fundamentally:

  • reducer pull driven

docs.title: 4. Sort Happens After Shuffle Fetch
docs.text:
Sorting occurs:

  • on reducer side
  • after partitions are fetched

NOT:

  • before network transfer

docs.title: 5. SortMergeJoin Itself Is Local
docs.text:
Actual join computation:

  • happens locally
  • after shuffle completes

docs.title: 6. AQE Optimizes Runtime Execution
docs.text:
AQE can:

  • coalesce partitions
  • optimize shuffle reads
  • dynamically adapt execution

based on:

  • actual runtime statistics

docs.title: 7. Most Join Cost Comes From Shuffle
docs.text:
The expensive part is:

  • network movement
  • disk spill
  • shuffle management

NOT:

  • merge computation itself
